answer:
# Answer

**A `frame-ancestors` directive declared in a policy delivered via an HTML `<meta>` element imposes zero framing restrictions. The directive has no effect in that position.** A document whose only framing policy is `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-ancestors 'none'">` remains embeddable by any origin, subject only to other mechanisms (an HTTP-header CSP, `X-Frame-Options`, COOP/COEP/CORP, etc.).

---

## 1. The rule (ask 2)

Normative statements in **Content Security Policy Level 3** (W3C):

- **§6.4.2 `frame-ancestors`** —
  > "The `frame-ancestors` directive MUST be ignored when contained in a policy declared via a `meta` element."

- **§3.3 The `<meta>` element**, Note —
  > "The `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` header is not supported inside a `meta` element. Neither are the `report-uri`, `frame-ancestors`, and `sandbox` directives."

Both statements also appear verbatim in the earlier CSP3 Working Draft (`https://www.w3.org/TR/2016/WD-CSP3-20160913/#meta-element`, §6.3.2 and §3.3), so this is not a recent editorial change; the same prohibition exists in CSP Level 2. MDN's `frame-ancestors` reference restates it as: "This directive is not supported in the `<meta>` element," and the Chrome CSP guide as: "This directive can't be used in `<meta>` tags."

Two corollaries that follow from the same sections and are frequently missed:

1. **`default-src` does not substitute.** §6.4.2's note: "`frame-ancestors` will not fall back to the `default-src` directive's value if one is specified. That is, a policy that declares `default-src 'none'` will still allow the resource to be embedded by anyone." This holds for header-delivered policies too — `default-src 'none'` never restricts framing.
2. **Ignoring the directive is not the same as discarding the policy.** The remaining directives in the same `meta` element (`script-src`, `img-src`, …) are parsed and enforced normally. Only the `frame-ancestors` token is dropped.

## 2. Why the rule exists (mechanism)

`frame-ancestors` is a **navigation directive**, not a resource-fetch directive (MDN's directive table: CSP version 2, directive type "Navigation directive"). The embedding decision is taken by the *embedder* — the parent browsing context — when it navigates a nested browsing context to the framed document's response. At that instant the user agent holds the response (status line, headers, body stream) but has not yet parsed the framed document's HTML, so no `<meta>` element can have been seen. The check is defined as the *frame-ancestors Navigation Response Check* (§6.4.2.1) and runs over the policies that arrived with the response. A `meta`-delivered policy only enters the document's policy container during HTML's "Content Security Policy state" `http-equiv` processing, i.e. mid-parse — structurally too late to influence an ancestor check that already happened. Hence the MUST-ignore rather than a soft failure.

This is why the directive is meaningful **only** as an HTTP response header, and why the same section lists `report-uri` and `sandbox` alongside it: all three govern things decided before or outside document parsing.

## 3. Decision table

| Delivery mechanism | Declared | Framing outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Security-Policy` **header** | `frame-ancestors 'none'` | Blocked |
| `Content-Security-Policy` **header** | `frame-ancestors 'self' https://example.org` | Allowed only for listed ancestors |
| `<meta http-equiv>` | `frame-ancestors 'none'` | **No effect — embeddable by anyone** |
| `<meta http-equiv>` | `frame-ancestors 'self' https://example.org` | **No effect — embeddable by anyone** |
| `<meta http-equiv>` | `default-src 'none'` (no `frame-ancestors`) | No effect on framing (no fallback) |
| `Content-Security-Policy` **header** | `default-src 'none'` (no `frame-ancestors`) | No effect on framing (no fallback) |
| No policy of any kind | — | Embeddable by anyone |
| `X-Frame-Options: DENY` header | — | Blocked (independent, legacy mechanism) |

## 4. Corrective guidance — how to actually restrict framing

The restriction must be moved to the response header. This is the only delivery mechanism that works:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
```

```http
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://example.org https://store.example.com
```

Syntax (CSP3 §6.4.2 ABNF):

```abnf
directive-name       = "frame-ancestors"
directive-value      = ancestor-source-list
ancestor-source-list = ( ancestor-source *( required-ascii-whitespace ancestor-source ) ) / "'none'"
ancestor-source      = scheme-source / host-source / "'self'"
```

Authoring constraints that fall out of the grammar and the surrounding notes:

- `'none'` and `'self'` **require** the single quotes. Bare `none` is an invalid source expression and is dropped.
- Only `scheme-source`, `host-source`, and `'self'` are legal `ancestor-source` values. Nonces, hashes, and `'unsafe-inline'` are not meaningful here.
- **Every ancestor in a nested chain is checked.** If any ancestor fails to match, the load is cancelled; leaf frames must list all ancestors when frames are nested.
- **Precedence with `X-Frame-Options`:** in browsers that support CSP2+, a header-delivered `frame-ancestors` governs; MDN documents `'none'` as "similar to `X-Frame-Options: deny` (which is also supported in older browsers)." Keep `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or `SAMEORIGIN`) in addition, purely for legacy user agents — it is belt-and-braces, not a substitute.

A correct page therefore looks like this (note: no `frame-ancestors` in the meta tag, because it would be silently discarded):

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Frame-Options: DENY
```

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <!-- OK: fetch directives are honoured in meta -->
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
          content="default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'">
    <!-- NOT PRESENT: frame-ancestors, report-uri, sandbox — all ignored in meta -->
  </head>
  <body>…</body>
</html>
```

## 5. Verification procedure

A competent engineer can confirm the rule in under five minutes with three pages.

**Setup.** Two origins: `https://parent.example/embed.html` (the embedder) and `https://child.example/framed.html` (the framed document). `embed.html` body:

```html
<iframe src="https://child.example/framed.html" width="400" height="200"></iframe>
```

**Case A — meta only (the case under test).** `framed.html` is served with **no** CSP header, and its head contains only:

```html
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-ancestors 'none'">
```

*Expected:* the iframe renders. Zero restrictions imposed. Confirms ask 1 = 0 and ask 3 = NO_EFFECT.

**Case B — header control.** Same body, but served with `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` and no meta tag.

*Expected:* the iframe is refused; the parent console reports that the frame was blocked by `frame-ancestors` (browsers phrase this as a "refused to display … in a frame" style message naming the CSP directive). Confirms the restriction is real when delivered correctly.

**Case C — mixed policy, proves directive-level ignoring rather than policy-level dropping.** `framed.html` head contains:

```html
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
      content="frame-ancestors 'none'; script-src 'none'">
```
plus `<script>document.body.dataset.ran = 'yes';</script>`.

*Expected:* the iframe **renders** (frame-ancestors ignored) **but** the inline script is blocked (`script-src 'none'` enforced). If the whole policy were discarded, the script would run — it must not.

**Case D — console signal.** Chromium emits a console warning along the lines of "The Content Security Policy directive 'frame-ancestors' is ignored when delivered via a `<meta>` element." This is browser behaviour, not spec text, and the exact wording varies by vendor and version; treat its presence as corroboration, not as the normative source.

**Pass criteria:** A renders, B is blocked, C renders with the script blocked. Any result where A is blocked would indicate the policy was in fact delivered by header (check for a proxy or framework injecting one) — not a counterexample to the rule.

## 6. Audit / lint check for an existing codebase

Flag any `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` whose `content` mentions a directive that is inert in meta. Regex for a grep-style sweep over templates and HTML:

```regex
<meta\b[^>]*\bhttp-equiv\s*=\s*["']?\s*content-security-policy\s*["']?[^>]*\bcontent\s*=\s*["'][^"']*\b(frame-ancestors|report-uri|sandbox)\b
```

A small Node/CI helper, returning one finding per offending tag:

```js
const INERT_IN_META = new Set(['frame-ancestors', 'report-uri', 'sandbox']);

const META_CSP =
  /<meta\b[^>]*\bhttp-equiv\s*=\s*["']?\s*content-security-policy\s*["']?[^>]*\bcontent\s*=\s*["']([^"']*)["'][^>]*>/gi;

export function findInertMetaDirectives(html, sourceName = '<inline>') {
  const findings = [];
  for (const match of html.matchAll(META_CSP)) {
    for (const raw of match[1].split(';')) {
      const name = raw.trim().split(/\s+/)[0]?.toLowerCase();
      if (name && INERT_IN_META.has(name)) {
        findings.push({
          source: sourceName,
          directive: name,
          severity: name === 'frame-ancestors' ? 'high' : 'medium',
          message:
            `'${name}' is ignored when delivered via <meta> ` +
            `(CSP3 §3.3, §6.4.2). Deliver it in the Content-Security-Policy ` +
            `HTTP response header instead.`,
        });
      }
    }
  }
  return findings;
}
```

Severity rationale: an inert `frame-ancestors` is a **high**-severity finding because it reads as clickjacking protection in code review while providing none; the page is fully framable and the reviewer's assumption is the vulnerability.

## 7. One-line statement of the rule

> In CSP Level 3, a `frame-ancestors` directive contained in a policy declared via a `<meta>` element MUST be ignored (§6.4.2); it is one of the directives (with `report-uri` and `sandbox`) that §3.3 explicitly excludes from meta delivery. It imposes **no** framing restrictions — zero — and the document may be embedded by any origin unless a header-delivered `frame-ancestors` or `X-Frame-Options` says otherwise.

ANSWER

One call to the Argon2 compression function G takes 2048 bytes of input in total (2 KiB).

DERIVATION

RFC 9106 (Argon2) defines the internal compression function G as a map on two blocks:

    G(X, Y)  ->  Z

where X and Y are each a 1024-byte block, and Z is a 1024-byte block. Both arguments are inputs; the output is not. Therefore:

    input bytes per call = sizeof(X) + sizeof(Y)
                         = 1024 B + 1024 B
                         = 2048 B
                         = 2 KiB

Equivalently, in the 64-bit words the function actually operates on (8 bytes per word):

    input words  = 2 blocks x 1024 B/block / 8 B/word = 256 words  (256 x 8 B = 2048 B)
    output words = 1 block  x 1024 B/block / 8 B/word = 128 words  (128 x 8 B = 1024 B)

The 128-word (1024-byte) output is deliberately excluded from the 2048-byte figure: the question asks for input bytes, and G's output is produced, not consumed.

QUANTITY TABLE (all mutually consistent)

    Quantity                              Value
    ------------------------------------  --------------------------
    Block size (X, Y, Z)                  1024 bytes
    Number of block inputs to G           2
    Total input bytes per G call          2048 bytes (= 2 KiB)
    Total input words per G call          256 (x 8 B = 2048 B)
    Output bytes per G call               1024 bytes (= 1 block)
    Output words per G call               128 (x 8 B = 1024 B)

WHAT COUNTS AS INPUT TO G, AND WHAT DOES NOT

Inside G, the first step forms R = X XOR Y, then the BLAKE2b-based permutation P is applied to the 8 rows of R and then to the 8 columns, and the result is combined with R again to give Z = P(rows/columns of R) XOR R. All of that intermediate material (R, the 16-word / 128-byte P registers, the round constants, the row/column index) is derived from or internal to the two blocks; it is not additional caller-supplied input. Hence the input total stays at 2048 bytes and does not grow with the internal round count.

The same holds for the overwrite/XOR variant of the function, G'(X, Y) = G(X, Y) XOR X XOR Y, used when a block is combined with its previously stored value (first pass overwrite vs. later-pass XOR). G' is fed exactly the same two 1024-byte blocks X and Y; the extra XOR operands are those same blocks, already counted. Input per call to G' is likewise 2048 bytes.

DISTRACTORS IN THE QUESTION, EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED

- t = 1 and m = 2 GiB are Argon2id cost parameters, not arguments to G. For context only: 2 GiB = 2^31 bytes = 2^21 = 2,097,152 blocks of 1024 bytes, which fixes the size of the memory matrix, not the arity or width of G. Neither figure enters the 2048-byte total.
- The 'MUST be supported' mandate for Argon2id is a conformance requirement and has no bearing on G's byte width.
- Parallelism p, salt, key, associated data, tag length: all outside G's interface.

FINAL VALUE

2048 bytes (2 KiB) of input per call to G.

question: Y43
answer:
# Answer

**UTF-8** (as defined by RFC 3629).

RFC 8259, Section 8.1 ("Character Encoding"), states normatively:

> JSON text exchanged between systems that are not part of a closed
> ecosystem MUST be encoded using UTF-8 [RFC3629].
>
> Previous specifications of JSON have not required the use of UTF-8
> when transmitting JSON text.  However, the vast majority of JSON-
> based software implementations have chosen to use the UTF-8 encoding,
> to the extent that it is the only encoding that achieves
> interoperability.
>
> Implementations MUST NOT add a byte order mark (U+FEFF) to the
> beginning of a networked-transmitted JSON text.  In the interests of
> interoperability, implementations that parse JSON texts MAY ignore
> the presence of a byte order mark rather than treating it as an
> error.

Source: RFC 8259, T. Bray (Ed.), "The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format," December 2017, Section 8.1, page 9. (Fetched from https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.txt and https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8259/.)

---

## 1. Reading the requirement precisely

The sentence has three parts that must all be honored; dropping any one of them changes the answer:

| Element | Text | Meaning for an implementer |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | "JSON text exchanged between systems that are not part of a closed ecosystem" | Applies to any JSON crossing a trust/ownership/implementation boundary: HTTP APIs, message brokers, service-to-service RPC, webhooks, file drops between teams or organizations, public data feeds. |
| Modality | **MUST** | A hard requirement (RFC 2119/BCP 14 keyword), not a recommendation. A non-UTF-8 JSON byte stream on such an interface is non-conforming. |
| Encoding | **UTF-8 [RFC3629]** | The specific encoding form is UTF-8 as profiled by RFC 3629 — not "Unicode," not "UTF-8 or UTF-16," not an implementation's default locale encoding. |

**The closed-ecosystem carve-out is real but narrow.** RFC 8259 leaves encodings other than UTF-8 permissible only where all communicating parties are inside one closed ecosystem and have agreed on the alternative out-of-band. It is never a safe default: an interface that is not *provably* closed must be treated as open, and therefore UTF-8.

**This is a change from the prior spec.** RFC 7159 §8.1 permitted UTF-8, UTF-16, or UTF-32 and named UTF-8 as the default. RFC 8259 removed that latitude for open interchange and made UTF-8 the sole conforming encoding. Any documentation, client library, or test suite still citing "UTF-8, UTF-16, or UTF-32" is describing RFC 7159, not RFC 8259.

---

## 2. What "UTF-8 [RFC3629]" concretely means at the byte level

Because the requirement cites RFC 3629 specifically, the encoding is RFC 3629's restricted UTF-8, not the older, looser definition. Conformance-relevant properties:

- **Sequence lengths.** U+0000–U+007F → 1 byte (`00`–`7F`); U+0080–U+07FF → 2 bytes (`C2`–`DF` lead); U+0800–U+FFFF → 3 bytes (`E0`–`EF` lead); U+10000–U+10FFFF → 4 bytes (`F0`–`F4` lead). Maximum 4 bytes per code point.
- **No 5- or 6-byte forms.** Lead bytes `F5`–`FF` are ill-formed. Maximum code point is U+10FFFF.
- **No overlong encodings.** A code point must use its shortest form (e.g. `/` is `2F`, never `C0 AF`).
- **No surrogate code points.** U+D800–U+DFFF must never appear as encoded bytes; RFC 3629 and Unicode §3.9 forbid representing a surrogate in UTF-8.
- **Escaped surrogates stay ASCII.** RFC 8259's grammar permits escapes such as `\uDEAD` (an unpaired surrogate) inside a JSON string. Such escapes are six ASCII bytes (`5C 75 44 45 41 44`); they are *not* encoded as a raw UTF-8 sequence for the surrogate. This keeps the byte stream valid UTF-8 even when the decoded string is not a valid Unicode scalar sequence.
- **Byte order mark.** U+FEFF encodes as `EF BB BF`. RFC 8259 forbids *adding* it to networked JSON (MUST NOT) and permits a parser to *ignore* one it receives (MAY). "MAY ignore" is a permission, not an obligation — a strict parser may reject it, so a generator that emits a BOM is producing output that some conforming peers will refuse.

---

## 3. Engineering consequences (backend layer)

1. **Serialization boundary.** Every byte the service writes as JSON must come from a UTF-8 encoder. In practice this means: no locale-dependent encoders, no `latin-1`/`cp1252` fallbacks, no implicit platform default. In Java, `getBytes()` without a charset is a defect — use `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`. In Python, `json.dumps(...).encode("utf-8")`, never `.encode()` with a mutated default. In Go, `encoding/json` already emits UTF-8; do not post-process with a transcoder.
2. **Deserialization boundary.** Accept UTF-8. Do not sniff UTF-16/UTF-32 by leading null bytes and silently transcode on an open interface: that masks a non-conforming producer and lets an encoding-confusion class of bug persist. If you must interoperate with a legacy closed peer, gate the transcode behind explicit, per-peer configuration and log it.
3. **HTTP.** `Content-Type: application/json` per RFC 8259 §11, whose registration lists `Optional parameters: n/a` and `Encoding considerations: binary`. There is no defined `charset` parameter for `application/json`; UTF-8 is already mandated, so `charset=utf-8` is redundant and technically an undefined parameter. Emit the bare media type; if you receive `charset=utf-8`, treat it as harmless; if you receive `charset=utf-16` or similar on an open interface, treat it as a conformance error rather than a hint.
4. **Message brokers and queues.** Set the payload as raw UTF-8 bytes, not as a platform string. Where the broker carries a content-type or schema-registry header, declare `application/json` and, for schema-backed topics, declare string fields as Unicode/UTF-8 so producers on other stacks cannot smuggle in another encoding. Validate on ingest at the consumer, not only at the producer.
5. **Databases and storage.** Store JSON in a UTF-8 column/collection (e.g. `jsonb`/`json` in a UTF-8 database, or `NVARCHAR`/UTF-8 collation where applicable). A database whose client encoding is not UTF-8 will silently mangle multi-byte characters at the driver boundary — a failure that surfaces far from its cause.
6. **Logs, error bodies, and headers.** Error responses and any JSON written into log lines or `Problem+JSON` bodies are also JSON text crossing a boundary; they get the same UTF-8 rule. Do not embed raw JSON in an HTTP header without escaping — non-ASCII is not legal there.
7. **BOM hygiene.** Strip a leading `EF BB BF` before parsing if your parser does not already, and never emit one. Watch for BOMs introduced by Windows-authored fixture files and by editors that "helpfully" add them.

---

## 4. Conformance checklist / verification procedure

A reviewer can run these checks against any interface in scope:

1. **Byte-level assertion.** For a payload containing a non-ASCII character (e.g. `é` U+00E9, `€` U+20AC, `𝄞` U+1D11E), assert the exact bytes: `é` → `C3 A9`; `€` → `E2 82 AC`; `𝄞` → `F0 9D 84 9E`. If you see `E9`, the producer used Latin-1; if you see `00 E9`, it used UTF-16BE; if `E9 00`, UTF-16LE.
2. **Strict decoder test.** Feed the payload to a strict UTF-8 validator that rejects overlongs, 5/6-byte forms, and surrogate byte sequences (Go's `utf8.Valid`, Python `bytes.decode("utf-8", "strict")`, Java `CharsetDecoder` with `CodingErrorAction.REPORT`). The validator must pass.
3. **BOM test.** Assert the first three bytes are not `EF BB BF` on outbound payloads. On inbound, assert the parser either strips the BOM or fails loudly — never silently mis-parses the first token.
4. **Media-type test.** Assert the outbound `Content-Type` is `application/json` (optionally with profile/vendor suffix), with no `charset` parameter.
5. **Round-trip test.** Serialize a document containing a non-BMP character, control characters, and a `\uXXXX`-escaped unpaired surrogate; re-read the raw bytes; confirm the bytes are unchanged and the decoded string values match.
6. **Cross-stack test.** Produce with one runtime and consume with another (e.g. JVM producer → Go consumer) to catch default-charset assumptions that same-stack tests hide.
7. **Closed-ecosystem exception register.** For any interface claimed to be exempt, require a written record naming every participant and the agreed alternative encoding. No record → the interface is open → UTF-8.

---

## 5. Common wrong answers, for disambiguation

- "UTF-8 or UTF-16 or UTF-32" — RFC 7159 language, superseded by RFC 8259.
- "UTF-8 with optional BOM" — the BOM is forbidden to be *added* on networked JSON; ignoring an incoming one is only a MAY.
- "Unicode" — not an encoding form; the requirement names a byte encoding, UTF-8.
- "ASCII / UTF-8 subset" — the JSON grammar permits any Unicode character in strings; ASCII-only output is a valid *subset* but is not the requirement.
- "Whatever the `Content-Type` charset says" — `application/json` has no charset parameter, and no header value can authorize a non-UTF-8 encoding on an open interface.

**Bottom line:** UTF-8, per RFC 3629, for every JSON text that crosses a boundary between systems not in a closed ecosystem — and no BOM.

question: Y44
answer:
ANSWER

RFC 8259, Section 6 ("Numbers"), states that when software implementing IEEE 754 binary64 (double precision) is used, integer JSON numbers in the inclusive range

    [-(2**53)+1, (2**53)-1]

are interoperable, in the sense that implementations will agree exactly on their numeric values.

Same range written in decimal, for convenience only (the RFC's own notation is the 2**53 form above):

    [-9007199254740991, 9007199254740991]

Both endpoints are inclusive; the RFC uses square brackets, `[` and `]`.

PROVENANCE (verbatim, RFC 8259 §6)

    This specification allows implementations to set limits on the range
    and precision of numbers accepted.  Since software that implements
    IEEE 754 binary64 (double precision) numbers [IEEE754] is generally
    available and widely used, good interoperability can be achieved by
    implementations that expect no more precision or range than these
    provide, in the sense that implementations will approximate JSON
    numbers within the expected precision.  A JSON number such as 1E400
    or 3.141592653589793238462643383279 may indicate potential
    interoperability problems, since it suggests that the software that
    created it expects receiving software to have greater capabilities
    for numeric magnitude and precision than is widely available.

    Note that when such software is used, numbers that are integers and
    are in the range [-(2**53)+1, (2**53)-1] are interoperable in the
    sense that implementations will agree exactly on their numeric
    values.

Source: RFC 8259 (T. Bray, Ed., December 2017), Section 6, page 8 — https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8259/ (also mirrored at https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8259/?include_text=1). The same endpoints are quoted in the nlohmann/json documentation (`number_integer_t`, `number_unsigned_t`, and the "number handling" feature page), which renders the range as $[-2^{53}+1, 2^{53}-1]$.

WHY THOSE ENDPOINTS (derivation, so the figure can be checked)

- binary64 has a 53-bit significand, so every integer n with |n| <= 2**53 is exactly representable; 2**53 + 1 is the smallest positive integer that is not.
- 2**53 = 9007199254740992.
- -(2**53)+1 = -9007199254740991 and (2**53)-1 = 9007199254740991.
- Both endpoints therefore have magnitude 2**53 - 1 <= 2**53, so all integers in the closed interval round-trip exactly through a double; the RFC uses 2**53 - 1 rather than 2**53 as the bound so that the whole stated range is exactly representable.

SCOPE AND CAVEATS (what the answer does and does not claim)

- The range is a statement about interoperability (exact agreement), not a validity limit on JSON syntax. RFC 8259 §6 explicitly permits implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted; integers outside this range may still be accepted, but exact agreement between sender and receiver is not guaranteed.
- The qualifier is "when such software is used", i.e. software implementing IEEE 754 binary64. An implementation using arbitrary-precision integers (e.g. a bignum-backed JSON library) is interoperable over a wider range, but that is not what the quoted sentence covers.
- The range applies to numbers that are integers (no fraction and no exponent part in value), not to JSON numbers generally; non-integer and very large-magnitude values such as 1E400 are called out in the same section as potential interoperability problems.
- "Interoperable" here means implementations agree exactly on the numeric value; it does not assert anything about lexical preservation of the original text (e.g. whether `1e2` is reserialized as `100`).

OPERATIONAL FORM (how a backend service should encode this bound)

If a service must guarantee cross-system exactness, enforce the bound at the serialization boundary and reject or widen the type for anything outside it:

    JSON_EXACT_INT_MIN = -(2**53) + 1   # -9007199254740991
    JSON_EXACT_INT_MAX =  (2**53) - 1   #  9007199254740991

    def is_interoperable_integer(n: int) -> bool:
        return JSON_EXACT_INT_MIN <= n <= JSON_EXACT_INT_MAX

For values outside the range, the interoperable options are: emit as a JSON string (with an explicit decimal-text contract), or require both peers to use arbitrary-precision integer handling; emitting them as bare JSON numbers is what the RFC flags as a potential interoperability problem.

question: Y45
answer:
# Answer

**UTF-8 and UTF-16.**

Every conforming XML processor is required to accept both of these encodings of Unicode, and is required to accept neither more nor fewer as a matter of mandate (anything else is optional).

---

## 1. Normative basis

**XML 1.0 (Fifth Edition), W3C Recommendation, 26 November 2008 — §2.2 Characters:**

> "The mechanism for encoding character code points into bit patterns may vary from entity to entity. All XML processors MUST accept the UTF-8 and UTF-16 encodings of Unicode [Unicode]; the mechanisms for signaling which of the two is in use, or for bringing other encodings into play, are discussed later, in 4.3.3 Character Encoding in Entities."

**Same specification — §4.3.3 Character Encoding in Entities:**

> "All XML processors MUST be able to read entities in both the UTF-8 and UTF-16 encodings. The terms \"UTF-8\" and \"UTF-16\" in this specification do not apply to related character encodings, including but not limited to UTF-16BE, UTF-16LE, or CESU-8."

**Corroboration — W3C Character Model for the World Wide Web 1.0 (§4.4, requirement context C018 note):**

> "The XML 1.0 specification [XML 1.0] requires all conforming XML processors to accept both UTF-16 and UTF-8."

The two passages above (from §2.2 and §4.3.3) are the normative requirement; the Character Model text is a non-normative restatement by the same standards body and agrees with it.

Note on scope of the obligation: §2.2 is stated of *all XML processors* — it is not conditioned on validating vs. non-validating (§5.1 of the same specification splits conforming processors into those two classes, but the encoding obligation in §2.2 and §4.3.3 binds both classes identically).

---

## 2. What the requirement does and does not cover

| Encoding / label | Status for an XML processor |
|---|---|
| **UTF-8** | MUST accept, with or without a BOM. |
| **UTF-16** | MUST accept. A UTF-16-encoded entity MUST begin with a BOM (§4.3.3), and the processor MUST be able to use that BOM to distinguish UTF-16 from UTF-8. |
| UTF-16BE, UTF-16LE (as distinct labels) | **Not** covered by the mandated terms "UTF-8"/"UTF-16" — expressly excluded by §4.3.3. May be supported; may be rejected if there is no external (transport-level) encoding information. |
| CESU-8 | Expressly excluded by §4.3.3. Optional. |
| UTF-32, ISO-8859-x, Shift_JIS, windows-1252, etc. | Optional. May be brought into play only via an encoding declaration or external transport information; not mandated. |
| US-ASCII | Not a separate mandate, but ASCII-only documents are trivially valid UTF-8 and must therefore be accepted. |

The requirement is a floor, not a ceiling. §4.3.3 continues (paraphrased from the same section): although a processor is required to read only entities in UTF-8 and UTF-16, other encodings are used around the world and a processor may be built to read them. Supporting ISO-8859-1 does not violate conformance; failing to support it does not violate conformance.

---

## 3. Related MUSTs that travel with the UTF-16 obligation

These are frequently missed in conformance reviews and belong in any compliance statement that cites the two-encoding rule:

1. **BOM requirement.** §4.3.3: "Entities encoded in UTF-16 MUST and entities encoded in UTF-8 MAY begin with the Byte Order Mark … (the ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE character, #xFEFF). This is an encoding signature, not part of either the markup or the character data of the XML document." Consequence: a UTF-16 BOM must be consumed as a signature and must not be surfaced as a U+FEFF character in character data; a UTF-8 BOM, if present, is likewise not content.
2. **BOM-based discrimination.** §4.3.3: "XML processors MUST be able to use this character to differentiate between UTF-8 and UTF-16 encoded documents."
3. **External parsed entity beginning with U+FEFF.** §4.3.3: if the replacement text of an external entity is to begin with U+FEFF and no text declaration is present, a BOM MUST be present, whether the entity is UTF-8 or UTF-16.
4. **Undecodable entity is a fatal error.** The specification requires a processor that meets an entity in an encoding it cannot process to report a fatal error rather than guess or silently misdecode. (Paraphrase; the sentence sits in §4.3.3 immediately after the optional-encoding discussion. The exact wording should be lifted from the Recommendation before being quoted in a contractual document.)
5. **Declaration/byte-stream disagreement.** Where no external transport information is available, it is a fatal error for an entity that carries an encoding declaration to be presented in an encoding other than the one named, and for an entity that begins with neither a BOM nor an encoding declaration to use an encoding other than UTF-8. (Paraphrase of the same paragraph in §4.3.3; verify wording against the Recommendation before quoting.)
6. **ASCII needs no declaration.** Because ASCII is a subset of UTF-8, ordinary ASCII-only entities do not strictly need an encoding declaration (same section).

---

## 4. Why the common wrong answers are wrong

- **"UTF-8 and UTF-16BE/UTF-16LE."** §4.3.3 explicitly says the terms UTF-8 and UTF-16 "do not apply to related character encodings, including but not limited to UTF-16BE, UTF-16LE, or CESU-8." A processor that accepts only UTF-16BE and UTF-16LE and rejects BOM-prefixed, endian-unspecified UTF-16 does not satisfy §2.2.
- **"UTF-8 and whatever the encoding declaration names."** The declaration mechanism does not create an obligation to support the named encoding; it only lets a document author bring other encodings into play with processors that choose to support them. §4.3.3's statement that a processor "is required to read only entities in the UTF-8 and UTF-16 encodings" is the boundary.
- **"UTF-8 and UTF-32."** UTF-32 is a Unicode encoding form and is permitted for specifications that require a unique encoding (Character Model requirement C018), but it is nowhere mandated for XML processors.
- **"UTF-8 alone."** Insufficient: §2.2 and §4.3.3 both name two encodings, and the BOM-discrimination MUST presupposes both.

---

## 5. Conformance verification procedure (test matrix)

A competent engineer can demonstrate compliance with the two-encoding rule using the following minimal vectors. Each is a well-formed XML document; the expected outcome is the processor's behaviour.

| # | Test input | Expected outcome | Clause |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | `<a/>` encoded UTF-8, no BOM, no encoding declaration | Accepted; document element `a` | §2.2, §4.3.3 |
| T2 | Same document, UTF-8 with BOM `EF BB BF` | Accepted; BOM not reported as content | §4.3.3 |
| T3 | `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><a/>` UTF-8 | Accepted | §4.3.3 |
| T4 | `FE FF` BOM + UTF-16BE bytes of `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-16"?><a/>` | Accepted; endianness taken from BOM | §2.2, §4.3.3 |
| T5 | `FF FE` BOM + UTF-16LE bytes of the same document | Accepted; endianness taken from BOM | §2.2, §4.3.3 |
| T6 | UTF-16 content with no BOM, ASCII-range only, `<?xml … encoding="UTF-16"?>` | Document is **non-conforming** (BOM MUST be present). Processor may recover via Appendix F heuristics but is not required to. | §4.3.3, App. F |
| T7 | ISO-8859-1 bytes with `encoding="ISO-8859-1"`, containing a byte ≥ 0x80 | Optional. Accept (correctly decoded) or report a fatal error. Silent misdecoding is a defect. | §4.3.3 |
| T8 | `encoding="UTF-16BE"`, no BOM | Optional; not part of the mandated pair. | §4.3.3 |
| T9 | Bytes are UTF-8 but declaration says `encoding="UTF-16"`, no transport-level information | Fatal error. | §4.3.3 |
| T10 | Declaration names an encoding the processor does not implement | Fatal error, reported — not silent substitution. | §4.3.3 |
| T11 | External parsed entity in UTF-16 whose replacement text begins with U+FEFF, no text declaration | Fatal error unless a BOM is present. | §4.3.3 |

Pass criterion for the two-encoding rule specifically: **T1–T5 accepted, and T9–T10 reported as fatal errors.** T6–T8 and T11 test adjacent obligations and are recorded for completeness.

---

## 6. Ready-to-use conformance clause

For a product specification, procurement document, or test report, the following single-sentence clause states the requirement exactly:

> "The XML processor shall accept, without error, well-formed XML documents encoded in UTF-8 (with or without a byte order mark) and in UTF-16 (either byte order, byte order mark present), in accordance with XML 1.0 Fifth Edition §2.2 and §4.3.3, and shall report a fatal error for any entity whose character encoding it is unable to process."

---

## 7. Version and cross-reference notes

- The same obligation appears unchanged in **XML 1.1** (§2.2 and §4.3.3), so the answer is stable across the two Recommendations; this answer is given for **Fifth Edition**, as asked.
- **RFC 7303 / IANA `application/xml`** names "Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0 (Fifth Edition)" as the published specification and its interoperability notes single out UTF-8 as the safest choice — consistent with, but not a substitute for, the normative §2.2 requirement.
- The IETF media-type drafts correctly note that `charset="utf-16"` entities begin with a BOM while `utf-16le`/`utf-16be` entities must not; that is a MIME-layer rule layered on top of, and consistent with, §4.3.3. It does not widen the set of encodings an XML processor is required to read.
- Quotations in §1 are verbatim from the fetched W3C Recommendation text. Passages in §3 marked "paraphrase" should be re-quoted from the Recommendation before being reproduced verbatim in a contractual or audited deliverable.

question: Y46
answer:
ANSWER: 48 bytes.

AUTHORITY
W3C WOFF2 File Format 2.0 description (WOFF2 File Format 2.0, W3C Recommendation / TR-WOFF2). The specification text states:

  "A complete WOFF2 file consists of several blocks of data: a 48-byte header, immediately followed (in this order) by a variable-size Table Directory, an optional Collection Directory (present only if the input font file is a font collection), a compressed font data block, an optional block of Extended Metadata, and an optional block of Private Data."

It also states that the Table Directory "is an array of WOFF2 table directory entries" and "Its size is dependent on the exact content." Therefore the Table Directory is not a fixed-size part.

HEADER FIELD-BY-FIELD SUM
WOFF2 header fields, from the specification:

| Field | Type | Bytes |
|---|---:|---:|
| signature | UInt32 | 4 |
| flavor | UInt32 | 4 |
| length | UInt32 | 4 |
| numTables | UInt16 | 2 |
| reserved | UInt16 | 2 |
| totalSfntSize | UInt32 | 4 |
| totalCompressedSize | UInt32 | 4 |
| majorVersion | UInt16 | 2 |
| minorVersion | UInt16 | 2 |
| metaOffset | UInt32 | 4 |
| metaLength | UInt32 | 4 |
| metaOrigLength | UInt32 | 4 |
| privOffset | UInt32 | 4 |
| privLength | UInt32 | 4 |
| TOTAL | | 48 |

Arithmetic: 4 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 48 bytes. This agrees with the specification's explicit "48-byte header" statement.

WHAT IS EXCLUDED AND WHY
1. Table Directory: variable-size per the specification ("variable-size Table Directory"; "Its size is dependent on the exact content"). It is not counted as a fixed-size part. Its length changes with numTables and with the encoding of each entry (flags, optional tag, Base128 origLength, optional transformLength), so any fixed number would be arbitrary.
2. Collection Directory: absent because there is no collection. The request specifies no collection; the Collection Directory is present only if the input font file is a font collection.
3. Extended Metadata block: absent. In a file without extended metadata, metaOffset = 0, metaLength = 0, metaOrigLength = 0, and no metadata bytes follow.
4. Private Data block: absent. In a file without private data, privOffset = 0, privLength = 0, and no private-data bytes follow.
5. Compressed font data block: variable-size by definition; it is not a fixed-size part.
6. Padding: explicitly excluded by the request; the specification allows at most three null bytes only where 4-byte alignment is specified.

CROSS-CHECK AGAINST THE SQLITE WAL HEADER
SQLite file-format documentation and the SQLite wal.c source state that "The WAL header is 32 bytes in size and consists of ... eight big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer values" (offsets 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28).

  SQLite WAL header: 8 x 4 bytes = 32 bytes.

This cross-check confirms only that both formats have separately specified, fixed-length headers: WOFF2 = 48 bytes, SQLite WAL = 32 bytes. The WAL figure is not added, subtracted, or otherwise folded into the WOFF2 figure. The request directs that the WAL header be used only as a cross-check of header sizes; it is not part of the WOFF2 file layout.

FINAL COMPUTATION
Fixed-size WOFF2 parts in the specified scenario:

  WOFF2 header = 48 bytes
  Collection Directory = 0 bytes (no collection)
  Extended Metadata = 0 bytes (none)
  Private Data = 0 bytes (none)
  Padding = 0 bytes (none)
  Table Directory = excluded, variable-size
  Compressed font data = excluded, variable-size

  Total fixed-size byte length = 48 bytes.

REPORTED WOFF2 VALUE: 48 bytes.

question: Y47
answer:
WOFF2 SIGNATURE FIELD VALUE AND REQUIRED USER-AGENT BEHAVIOR
(Grounded in W3C WOFF File Format 2.0, §3.2 "WOFF2 Header"; identical wording in the 2015 WD, 2016 CR, 2018 REC and the current 2024 REC https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WOFF2-20240808/)

=====================================================================
1. NORMATIVE ANSWER (verbatim from the specification)
=====================================================================
"The signature field in the WOFF2 header MUST contain the value of 0x774F4632 ('wOF2'), which distinguishes it from WOFF 1.0 files. If the field does not contain this value, user agents MUST reject the file as invalid."

Ask 1 — exact signature field value: 0x774F4632
Ask 2 — required behavior on mismatch: user agents MUST reject the file as invalid.

=====================================================================
2. BYTE-LEVEL REPRESENTATION OF THE SIGNATURE
=====================================================================
The signature is the FIRST field of the WOFF2 header, at file offset 0, typed UInt32, stored BIG-ENDIAN (network byte order, as are all WOFF2 header integers).

  Field name : signature
  Type       : UInt32 (unsigned 32-bit integer)
  Offset     : 0x00000000 (bytes 0..3)
  Length     : 4 bytes
  Value      : 0x774F4632
  Decimal    : 2001684018  (within UInt32 range; also < 2^31, so positive even as a signed int32)

  Byte order on disk (offset : hex : ASCII):
    0 : 0x77 : 'w'
    1 : 0x4F : 'O'
    2 : 0x46 : 'F'
    3 : 0x32 : '2'
  On-disk byte sequence: 77 4F 46 32   (ASCII "wOF2")

  Reading the four bytes as a big-endian unsigned integer reproduces the constant exactly:
    (0x77 << 24) | (0x4F << 16) | (0x46 << 8) | 0x32
    = 0x77000000 | 0x004F0000 | 0x00004600 | 0x00000032
    = 0x774F4632

Warning on endianness: a little-endian read of the same bytes yields 0x32464F77, which is NOT the signature. Implementations must read the field as big-endian (or compare the four raw bytes in file order), never as a native-endian integer.

=====================================================================
3. HOW IT IS DISTINGUISHED FROM OTHER FORMATS (why the value is this constant)
=====================================================================
  WOFF 2.0 : 0x774F4632  'wOF2'  <- required value
  WOFF 1.0 : 0x774F4646  'wOFF'  (differs only in the final byte: 0x32 vs 0x46)
  sfnt/TrueType : 0x00010000, 'true' (0x74727565), 'typ1'
  OpenType/CFF : 'OTTO' (0x4F54544F)
  Font collection: 'ttcf' (0x74746366)
The specification states the signature's purpose explicitly: it "distinguishes it from WOFF 1.0 files." A 'wOFF' file is a valid WOFF 1.0 file and MUST NOT be accepted as WOFF2; a 'wOF2' file MUST NOT be treated as WOFF 1.0.

=====================================================================
4. WHAT "MUST REJECT THE FILE AS INVALID" MEANS OPERATIONALLY
=====================================================================
The requirement is normative (RFC 2119 MUST) and is a hard failure. A conforming user agent, upon reading bytes 0..3 and finding a value other than 0x774F4632, must:

  a. Not recognize/classify the resource as WOFF2. The file is invalid as WOFF2, full stop.
  b. Abort processing immediately, before any further parsing: no table-directory read, no Brotli decompression of CompressedFontData, no metadata block decode, no reconstruction of an sfnt, no caching of a decoded font, no font registration.
  c. Not load or use the font for rendering/layout/shaping. A font face that fails this check must be treated as a failed font load (in CSS terms, the @font-face / FontFace load fails and the font does not participate in font matching; the UA proceeds as it would for any unavailable font, e.g. fallback fonts).
  d. Not silently "repair" the value, guess the format from later bytes, or attempt a decode anyway. There is no lenient path in the specification for the signature field.

Because the check is on the first four bytes, it is O(1) and requires zero decompression — it is the cheapest possible guard and also protects the decoder from being handed non-WOFF2 content (including decompression-bomb payloads) mislabeled with the font/woff2 media type.

Scope note on 'reject': rejecting the file as WOFF2 does not forbid a user agent from independently recognizing the same bytes as some other format using that format's own signature rules (e.g. a 'wOFF' file is still a valid WOFF 1.0 file; a 'ttcf'/'OTTO'/'true' file is still that format). What is forbidden is accepting it *as WOFF2*.

=====================================================================
5. CONTRAST WITH NEIGHBORING HEADER RULES (what is NOT a rejection trigger)
=====================================================================
These are stated in the same specification paragraph and must not be conflated with the signature rule:
  - reserved field: "A valid WOFF 2.0 file MUST have the reserved field set to 'zero', a decoder MUST NOT reject a downloaded font file if the reserved header value is not zero." -> encoder-side requirement only; decoders are lenient.
  - totalSfntSize: "User agents MUST NOT reject correctly decoded font file if the resulting font file size doesn't match the totalSfntSize value..." -> informational/reference only.
  - signature: MUST contain 0x774F4632; otherwise MUST reject. -> the only one of the three that is a mandatory decoder-side rejection.

For context, the full 48-byte WOFF2 header (the signature is the first field):
  Offset  Size  Field                Notes
  0       4     signature            MUST be 0x774F4632 'wOF2'
  4       4     flavor               sfnt version of the input font
  8       4     length               total size of the WOFF2 file
  12      2     numTables            number of table directory entries
  14      2     reserved             MUST be 0 in a valid file; decoders MUST NOT reject if nonzero
  16      4     totalSfntSize        reference only; mismatch MUST NOT cause rejection
  20      4     totalCompressedSize  length of the compressed data block
  24      2     majorVersion
  26      2     minorVersion
  28      4     metaOffset
  32      4     metaLength
  36      4     metaOrigLength
  40      4     privOffset
  44      4     privLength
  (4+4+4+2+2+4+4+2+2+4+4+4+4+4 = 48 bytes)

=====================================================================
6. REFERENCE CHECK (copy-pasteable)
=====================================================================
JavaScript (browser/Node, works on ArrayBuffer/TypedArray):

  const WOFF2_SIGNATURE = 0x774f4632; // 'wOF2'

  function readU32BE(bytes, off) {
    // >>> 0 forces an unsigned 32-bit result
    return ((bytes[off] << 24) | (bytes[off + 1] << 16) |
            (bytes[off + 2] << 8) | bytes[off + 3]) >>> 0;
  }

  function isWoff2(bytes) {
    if (!(bytes instanceof Uint8Array)) bytes = new Uint8Array(bytes);
    if (bytes.byteLength < 4) return false;         // truncated: cannot be a WOFF2 file
    return readU32BE(bytes, 0) === WOFF2_SIGNATURE;
  }

  // Usage at the top of a decoder pipeline:
  //   if (!isWoff2(buf)) throw new Error('Invalid WOFF2 file: bad signature');
  //   ... only now parse the table directory and Brotli-decompress ...

Byte-wise equivalent (language-agnostic, avoids endianness mistakes entirely):

  function isWoff2Bytes(b0, b1, b2, b3) {
    return b0 === 0x77 && b1 === 0x4F && b2 === 0x46 && b3 === 0x32;
  }

C-style pseudo-code for a decoder entry point:

  uint32_t sig = read_u32_be(file, 0);
  if (sig != 0x774F4632u) {
      return WOFF2_ERR_INVALID_SIGNATURE;   // reject as invalid; no further parsing
  }
  // proceed: table directory, then Brotli decompression of CompressedFontData

=====================================================================
7. TEST VECTORS
=====================================================================
  Bytes 0..3            As UInt32 BE   Expected result
  77 4F 46 32           0x774F4632     ACCEPT as WOFF2 (required value)
  77 4F 46 46           0x774F4646     REJECT as invalid (this is WOFF 1.0 'wOFF')
  32 46 4F 77           0x32464F77     REJECT (little-endian misread of 'wOF2' — signals a byte-order bug)
  00 01 00 00           0x00010000     REJECT as WOFF2 (bare TrueType sfnt)
  4F 54 54 4F           0x4F54544F     REJECT as WOFF2 ('OTTO' / CFF OpenType)
  74 74 63 66           0x74746366     REJECT as WOFF2 ('ttcf' collection)
  77 4F 46              (truncated)    REJECT (fewer than 4 bytes)
  (empty file)          n/a            REJECT (fewer than 4 bytes)
  Case sensitivity: the check is on byte values, not on text; there is no case-insensitive matching. 0x77 0x6F 0x46 0x32 ('woF2') is NOT the signature and MUST be rejected.

=====================================================================
8. ONE-LINE ANSWERS
=====================================================================
  Signature value required : 0x774F4632 — the four bytes 77 4F 46 32, ASCII 'wOF2', at offset 0, big-endian UInt32.
  On mismatch              : the user agent MUST reject the file as invalid (no decode, no load, no use).

question: Y49
answer:
ANSWER

2^53 - 1 elements

(i.e. 9,007,199,254,740,991 elements = 9007199254740991, which equals Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.)

SOURCE AND DERIVATION

Governing clause: ECMA-262 15th Edition (June 2024), §6.1.4 "The String Type":

  "The String type is the set of all ordered sequences of zero or more 16-bit unsigned
  integer values ("elements") up to a maximum length of 2^53 - 1 elements."

Why the ASCII form is 2^53 and not 253: in the printed/PDF edition the exponent is typeset as a superscript, so the plain-text extraction of the PDF renders "2⁵³ - 1" as the run-together string "253 - 1". The same clause served as HTML at 262.ecma-international.org/15.0 disambiguates the typesetting by writing it as "2**53 - 1". The value whose exponent is printed as a superscript is therefore 2^53 (9007199254740992), and the stated maximum length is that value minus one. The ASCII-exponent rendering requested is thus:

  2^53 - 1

Unit: "elements", per the same clause, which defines elements as 16-bit unsigned integer values and then states: "The length of a String is the number of elements (i.e., 16-bit values) within it." So the maximum length is counted in UTF-16 code units, not in code points, characters, or grapheme clusters.

ARITHMETIC CHECK

  2^10 = 1024
  2^20 = 1,048,576
  2^30 = 1,073,741,824
  2^50 = 1,125,899,906,842,624
  2^53 = 2^50 * 8 = 9,007,199,254,740,992
  2^53 - 1 = 9,007,199,254,740,991

Binary form of the maximum: 53 ones (111...111, 53 bits). This is exactly the largest integer n for which every integer in [0, n] is exactly representable as an IEEE-754 binary64 Number, which is why the limit is set there: the length of a String is exposed as a Number (String.prototype.length, §22.1.4.1, returns an integral Number), so a length of 2^53 would already be unrepresentable as an exact Number.

SCOPE NOTES (what the number does and does not claim)

- This is the normative limit of the String type in ECMA-262 15th Edition. It is an upper bound on the abstract type, not a guarantee any implementation reaches: engines impose their own, much lower, practical limits (e.g. V8's maximum string length is on the order of 2^29 - 24 code units on 64-bit builds; SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore have their own caps). Those are implementation limits, not the specification's, and are not the answer to this question.
- The count is in elements = UTF-16 code units. A string of 2^53 - 1 code units could contain at most that many code points, but a non-BMP code point occupies two elements, so the maximum number of code points in a String is at most 2^53 - 1 and in general fewer; the specification does not bound code points separately.
- ECMA-262 does not restrict element values: any sequence of 16-bit unsigned integers is a valid String value, including unpaired surrogates ("ill-formed" UTF-16). The maximum length is therefore a pure sequence-length bound and is independent of well-formedness or normalization.
- The limit is unchanged from earlier editions (e.g. 6th Edition §6.1.4 states the same 2^53 - 1), and ECMAScript 2024 made no change to it.

DELIVERABLE FORM

Value: 2^53 - 1
Unit: elements
Exact decimal (if a numeric literal is needed): 9007199254740991
Superscripted quantity being exponentiated, in ASCII: 2^53

FORMAT COMPLIANCE

- Ask 2 ("Answer in elements"): satisfied — the answer is expressed as a count of elements (16-bit unsigned integer values / UTF-16 code units), as defined in §6.1.4.
- Ask 3 ("using ASCII exponent notation for the value whose exponent is printed as a superscript"): satisfied — the power is written as 2^53 with a caret, not as a superscript glyph and not as the flattened PDF artifact "253".

question: Y50
answer:
ANSWER

1. Built-in `clear` — attached to **Go 1.21** (toolchain-level identifier: `go1.21.0`).
2. Built-in `min` and `max` — attached to **Go 1.21** (toolchain-level identifier: `go1.21.0`). `min` and `max` share a single version because they were introduced together in the same release.

All three built-ins (`clear`, `min`, `max`) arrived in the same release, Go 1.21. Any answer that separates them by a version is wrong.

---

EVIDENCE, IN ORDER OF AUTHORITY

**A. The specification's own version history (the direct answer for all three).**
go.dev/ref/spec, section "Version history of the language", entry for Go 1.21, states verbatim:

> Go 1.21
> The set of predeclared functions includes the new functions
> min, max, and clear.

This single sentence is the authoritative statement that all three built-ins are attached to Go 1.21. It is the sentence to quote if only one citation is permitted.

**B. The inline version annotation on the min/max section (the direct answer for ask 2).**
go.dev/ref/spec, "Built-in functions" → "Min and max", carries the bracketed version tag in the body text:

> The built-in functions min and max compute the smallest—or largest, respectively—value of a fixed number of arguments of ordered types. There must be at least one argument **[Go 1.21]**.

The `[Go 1.21]` tag is the specification's own mechanism for marking the release in which a language feature was added; it is literally the version "attached to" `min` and `max` in the document.

**C. The package reference annotation on clear (and min/max).**
pkg.go.dev/builtin, which renders the documentation of the predeclared identifiers, shows under `func clear`:

> func clear ¶
> added in go1.21.0

and under `func min`:

> func min ¶
> added in go1.21.0

with `func max` immediately preceding `min` and carrying the same `go1.21.0` annotation line at the head of its block. This is the same fact expressed at toolchain granularity (`go1.21.0`), which is why the canonical form in this deliverable is "Go 1.21" with `go1.21.0` given as its toolchain identifier.

**D. The Go 1.21 release notes (corroboration).**
go.dev/doc/go1.21, "Changes to the language":

> Go 1.21 adds three new built-ins to the language. The new functions min and max compute the smallest (or largest, for max) value of a fixed number of given arguments... The new function clear deletes all elements from a map or zeroes all elements of a slice.

The same release notes also record the derivative library surface, `reflect.Value.Clear`, described as corresponding "to the new clear built-in added to the language" — a second, independent in-release confirmation that `clear` is new in 1.21.

**E. The builtin package source (primary source code).**
go.dev/src/builtin/builtin.go declares the three functions with no earlier provenance:

> // The clear built-in function clears maps and slices.
> func clear[T ~[]Type | ~map[Type]Type1](t T)

> func max[T cmp.Ordered](x T, y ...T) T
> func min[T cmp.Ordered](x T, y ...T) T

The source file itself carries no version comment; the version attribution lives in the specification and in the generated package docs (C above). This is expected and is not a contradiction.

---

HOW TO REPRODUCE / VERIFY (procedure)

1. Open https://go.dev/ref/spec and confirm the document header reads a language version at or after go1.21 (the copy consulted for this answer read "Language version go1.27 (May 26, 2026)"). A spec older than 1.21 will not contain these built-ins at all — see the caveat below.
2. Search the page for `Go 1.21`. Two hits matter: the "Version history of the language" entry quoting "min, max, and clear", and the `[Go 1.21]` tag inside "Min and max".

Search the page for `id="Clear"` / "func clear" in "Built-in functions" to confirm the function is specified; its version attribution is the version-history entry from step 2 (the `clear` section carries no separate inline tag, which is why the version-history sentence, not an inline tag, is the citation for ask 1).

## Answer

For a SQLite database file using the smallest allowed page size, the largest reserved-space byte count allowed by the usable-size rule is **32 bytes per page**.

## Derivation from the SQLite Database File Format document

### 1. Smallest allowed page size

Section 1.2, 'Pages', states:

> 'The size of a page is a power of two between 512 and 65536 inclusive. All pages within the same database are the same size. The page size for a database file is determined by the 2-byte integer located at an offset of 16 bytes from the beginning of the database file.'

Therefore:

- minimum page size = **512 bytes**
- the page-size value is stored in the 2-byte integer at file offset 16

### 2. Usable-size rule

Section 1.3.4, 'Reserved bytes per page', states:

> 'The "reserved space" size in the 1-byte integer at offset 20 is the number of bytes of space at the end of each page to reserve for extensions. This value is usually 0. The value can be odd.'
>
> 'The "usable size" of a database page is the page size specified by the 2-byte integer at offset 16 in the header less the "reserved" space size recorded in the 1-byte integer at offset 20 in the header. The usable size of a page might be an odd number. However, the usable size is not allowed to be less than 480. In other words, if the page size is 512, then the reserved space size cannot exceed 32.'

So the constraint is:

```text
usable_size = page_size - reserved_bytes
usable_size >= 480
```

Rearranged for a fixed page size:

```text
reserved_bytes <= page_size - 480
```

### 3. Calculation

Apply the minimum page size:

```text
page_size        = 512 bytes
usable_size_min  = 480 bytes

reserved_max = page_size - usable_size_min
             = 512 - 480
             = 32 bytes
```

Therefore:

```text
reserved_bytes ∈ {0, 1, 2, ..., 32}
maximum reserved_bytes = 32
```

The value can be odd per the document, so no alignment restriction changes this result.

### 4. Boundary verification

| reserved bytes | usable size = 512 − reserved | Valid? |
|---:|---:|:---|
| 0 | 512 | yes |
| 31 | 481 | yes |
| **32** | **480** | **yes — exactly at the minimum** |
| 33 | 479 | **no — below 480** |
| 255 | 257 | no |

Thus 32 is the largest permitted value, not merely a permitted value. The 1-byte header field at offset 20 can represent values up to 255, but that field-width limit does not bind for a 512-byte page: the usable-size rule limits reserved space to 32 before the field width becomes relevant.

### 5. Result in terms of the file header

For a 512-byte-page database:

```text
Offset 16, 2-byte page-size field  = 512
Offset 20, 1-byte reserved field  <= 32
```

The maximum legal header value at offset 20 is therefore **32**.

### 6. Practical SQLite check

A database created with the minimum page size and the maximum legal reserved space uses:

```sql
PRAGMA page_size = 512;
PRAGMA reserve_size = 32;
```

This leaves usable size = 512 − 32 = 480, which satisfies the document's rule. Setting `reserve_size = 33` would leave usable size = 479 and violate the rule.

## Final value

**32 bytes** of reserved space per page.

# Standards determination — IANA service name for a TCP port in the Dynamic and/or Private Ports range

Function: Standards Engineer (registry-scope interpretation). Deliverable is this written determination; nothing here requires a repository, shell or build step.

## 1. Answer

**Verdict (ask 4):** No IANA-assigned service name exists for any TCP port in the Dynamic and/or Private Ports range, 49152-65535. The range is outside the registry's assignment scope by rule, so the answer is a rule-derived "none", not an observation that some particular entry happens to be missing.

**Value (ask 1):** none — there is no IANA-assigned service name to report.

The answer is **port-independent**. Because the scope rule excludes the whole 16,384-value block, the determination does not require knowing which port in 49152-65535 the engineer means, and the absence of a port number in the request is not a defect.

## 2. Governing text (quoted verbatim from the fetched sources)

**S1 — IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry, scope note.** Page 'Last Updated 2026-11-19'; fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:18Z; sha256 a1ccda52c795…:

> "Port numbers are divided into three ranges, with their uses and assignment procedures specified in Section 8.1.2 of RFC 6335:
> System Ports (0-1023) are assigned using the IETF Review or IESG Approval procedures.
> User Ports (1024-49151) are assigned using the IETF Review, IESG Approval, or Expert Review procedures.
> Dynamic and/or Private Ports (49152-65535) are not assigned."

**S2 — RFC 6335, Section 6 (Port Number Ranges).** Fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:18Z; sha256 7c02af86a6f9…:

> "TCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP, and DCCP use 16-bit namespaces for their port number registries. The port registries for all of these transport protocols are subdivided into three ranges of numbers [RFC1340] …
> o the System Ports, also known as the Well Known Ports, from 0-1023 (assigned by IANA)
> o the User Ports, also known as the Registered Ports, from 1024-49151 (assigned by IANA)
> o the Dynamic Ports, also known as the Private or Ephemeral Ports, from 49152-65535 (never assigned)"

**S3 — RFC 6335, Section 6, on port states:**

> "Of the assignable port ranges (System Ports and User Ports, i.e., port numbers 0-49151), individual port numbers are in one of three states at any given time:
> o Assigned: …
> o Unassigned: … available for assignment upon request …
> o Reserved: … not available for regular assignment; they are 'assigned to IANA' for special purposes. Reserved port numbers include values at the edges of each range, …"

**S4 — RFC 6335, Section 8.1.2 (the section the registry itself cites):**

> "Ports in the Dynamic Ports range (49152-65535) have been specifically set aside for local and dynamic use and cannot be assigned through IANA. Application software may simply use any dynamic port that is available on the local host, without any sort of assignment. On the other hand, application software MUST NOT assume that a specific port number in the Dynamic Ports range will always be available for communication at all times, and a port number in that range hence MUST NOT be used as a service identifier."

## 3. Why this is the defensible answer — the rule, not the absence of a row

Three independent grounds, all from the registry's own normative text:

1. **Registry scope note (S1):** the range is "not assigned" — stated as a range property, not as a per-entry fact.
2. **RFC 6335 §6 (S2):** the dynamic range is "never assigned" — the word *never* is a policy statement, not a snapshot.
3. **RFC 6335 §8.1.2 (S4):** such ports "cannot be assigned through IANA" and "MUST NOT be used as a service identifier" — a prohibition, not an omission.

**The decisive scope argument (S3):** the Assigned / Unassigned / Reserved trichotomy is explicitly defined *only* over "the assignable port ranges (System Ports and User Ports, i.e., port numbers 0-49151)". Therefore, inside 49152-65535 the term "Unassigned" is not even applicable. The correct characterisation is **out of assignment scope**. This is what makes the answer defensible: it is *not* "port N is currently unassigned, so check back later" — no future registry action can create an assignment for a port in this range without an RFC that changes RFC 6335 itself.

## 4. Temporal applicability — "as in force on 2026-11-21" (ask 3)

- The registry page fetched at **2026-11-23T11:49:18Z** still reports **"Last Updated 2026-11-19"**. Since a fetch two days *after* the requested date shows no update later than 2026-11-19, no registry change was recorded on 2026-11-20, 2026-11-21 or 2026-11-22. The version in force on 2026-11-21 is therefore exactly the 2026-11-19 version quoted here.
- RFC 6335 (August 2011; its page header reads "Best Current Practice") is the normative reference the registry cites in its own "Reference" field. The inline-errata rendering reproduces §6 and §8.1.2 verbatim, so errata in force do not alter the range definitions.
- Residual risk, stated rather than hidden: an amendment published *and* reverted within 2026-11-20..22 would be invisible to this method. None is in evidence, and the conclusion rests on RFC-level range policy rather than on a volatile per-entry data value, so the exposure is negligible.

## 5. Scope of the rule and range arithmetic

- **Transport (ask 2):** the registry is shared; §6 opens "TCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP, and DCCP use 16-bit namespaces … subdivided into three ranges." The TCP qualifier neither narrows nor changes the result.
- **Arithmetic, checked:** System 0-1023 = 1,024 ports; User 1024-49151 = 48,128 ports; Dynamic 49152-65535 = 16,384 ports. 1,024 + 48,128 + 16,384 = 65,536 = 2^16, so the three ranges tile the 16-bit space exactly and every value in 49152-65535 lies inside the "never assigned" block. There is no gap or overlap that could place a port in a different regime.

## 6. Edge cases and near-miss answers, handled explicitly

**(a) Edge values that may be Reserved.** The S3 passage continues "Reserved port numbers include values at the edges of each range, …" (truncated in the fetched excerpt; the list is not reproduced here rather than guessed). If the queried port is a range-edge value such as 49152 or 65535, it may be recorded as Reserved *to IANA for special purposes*. That is **not** a service-name assignment: Reserved means "assigned to IANA", not to a service, and the registry scope note still says the range is not assigned. **Answer unchanged: no IANA-assigned service name.**

**(b) Table rendering.** Even if a tabular view renders a row for a port in this range, such a row carries no assignee, registration date, or service name constituting an assignment; the scope note governs over any rendering. In particular, do not read a displayed "Unassigned" as an assignment state — S3 confines that term to 0-49151.

**(c) Service names without port numbers.** The registry does contain service names registered with blank port fields (e.g. the `dns-update` and `dns-update-tls` rows visible in the registry search view). Those are **not** assignments to a dynamic-range port; they are names intended to be located via SRV. So: "is there a registered service name that *owns* my dynamic port?" — No. "Can I have a registered service name while my server listens on a dynamic port?" — Yes, via SRV (see §7).

**(d) De-assignment.** RFC 6335 §8.2 de-assignment marks a returned port Reserved and operates on *granted assignments*, i.e. within 0-49151. It cannot produce a dynamic-range assignment either.

## 7. What the engineer should do with this

- If a specific port is in hand and a label is attached to it, that label is local convention, vendor documentation, or unregistered de facto use — **not** an IANA assignment, and per §8.1.2 the port "MUST NOT be used as a service identifier".
- Compliant options: (i) obtain a **User Port** assignment in 1024-49151; (ii) register a **service name without a port number** and advertise the dynamic port through DNS SRV (RFC 2782) — RFC 6335 §5 anticipates exactly this: service names "SHOULD be registered with IANA … The details of using Service Names in SRV Service Labels are specified in the DNS SRV specification [RFC2782]"; (iii) use a private namespace for purely internal naming.
- Carry the registry's own disclaimer into any incident or firewall decision: traffic to or from a port does not by itself indicate the assigned service, and "Assigned ports both System and User ports SHOULD NOT be used without or prior to IANA registration."

## 8. Citation ledger

| ID | Source | Locator | Fetch / hash | Used for |
|----|--------|---------|--------------|----------|
| S1 | IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry | https://www.iana.org/assignments/service-names-port-numbers | 2026-11-23T11:49:18Z, sha256 a1ccda52c795 | Range scope note; "Last Updated 2026-11-19" |
| S2 | RFC 6335 §6 | https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6335.html | 2026-11-23T11:49:18Z, sha256 7c02af86a6f9 | Range boundaries; "never assigned" |
| S3 | RFC 6335 §6 | same as S2 | same as S2 | Assigned/Unassigned/Reserved limited to 0-49151 |
| S4 | RFC 6335 §8.1.2 | https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6335/ | 2026-11-23T11:49:18Z, sha256 76231ab3f7ba | "cannot be assigned through IANA"; "MUST NOT be used as a service identifier" |

## 9. Limits of this answer

This determination interprets the registry's scope rule; it does not identify what any particular live service on a dynamic-range port happens to be, and it deliberately does not supply a "name" that the registry does not assign. It would be superseded only by an RFC updating RFC 6335's range definitions or by a registry scope note that assigns ports in 49152-65535 — neither is present in the sources in force on 2026-11-21.

COMPLIANCE MEMORANDUM — IANA 'example' media type: registered subtypes and governing rule, as in force 2026-11-21

1. BOTTOM LINE

No subtype is registered under the IANA 'example' media type — not as of 2026-11-21 and not on any other date. The registry does not merely happen to be empty; it is prohibited by rule from ever being non-empty. The answer to "which subtype under 'example' is registered for a new documentation example" is therefore: none, and none can be. For a new documentation example the author uses an arbitrary, unregistered subtype string that is syntactically valid, e.g. `example/foo` or `example/notification-v2`; no IANA assignment exists or is obtainable for it.

2. THE RULE — VERBATIM REGISTRY TEXT

2.1 IANA Media Types registry, entry for the 'example' type (https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types):

  "The 'example' media type is used for examples. Any subtype following the media type syntax may be used in those examples. No subtype can be registered with IANA. For more information see RFC 4735."

  followed by the note:

  "Note: The occurrence of an 'example' media type as a media type outside of examples, e.g. in a Content-Type header, is an error and should be reported to the implementor."

2.2 IANA Top-Level Media Types registry (https://www.iana.org/assignments/top-level-media-types), 'example' row:

  Name: example | Reference: RFC 4735 | Registry of Subtypes: Example Media Types | Comments: "no registrations, for examples only"

  Registry metadata on that page: Created 2024-06-25; Last Updated 2025-03-18; Registration Procedure(s): Standards Action; Reference: RFC 9694.

2.3 The normative source, RFC 4735 ("Example Media Types", October 2006), Section 3, registration of the 'example' media type:

  "Type name: example.
   Subtype name: any subtype may be used with the 'example' type. However, IANA MUST NOT register any subtypes for the 'example' media type.
   Required parameters: as invented by the user.
   Optional parameters: as invented by the user.
   Encoding considerations: as invented by the user.
   Security considerations: The 'example' media type is defined for use in documentation only. It MUST NOT be implemented. ...
   Intended usage: LIMITED USE.
   Restrictions on usage: This type is intended only for use in documents providing examples involving specification of some media type, where the actual media type used is irrelevant."

  RFC 4735 is a Standards Track document; its change controller is the IETF. The top-level registry still cites RFC 4735 as the reference for 'example' in the snapshot consulted, i.e. no successor document has superseded it.

3. WHY THIS HOLDS FOR 2026-11-21 SPECIFICALLY

The registry snapshot available for this review was retrieved 2026-11-23T11:53Z, two days after the as-of date, so the date question must be answered explicitly rather than assumed:

(a) Invariance. RFC 4735 §3 uses a normative prohibition ("IANA MUST NOT register any subtypes for the 'example' media type"). A prohibition constrains the registry on every date in the interval during which it is in force. It is in force on 2026-11-21 because the top-level registry still lists RFC 4735 as the reference for 'example' in the 2026-11-23 snapshot and no superseding RFC appears in any consulted source. Therefore the set of subtypes registered under 'example' on 2026-11-21 is empty, exactly as on 2026-11-23.

(b) Version pinning. The Top-Level Media Types registry carrying the 'example' row shows "Last Updated 2025-03-18" — before the as-of date. No post-2025-03-18 modification to that row is evidenced, and none is possible for the 'example' subtype set without an RFC change.

(c) Residual risk, stated for the record. If one insisted on a byte-exact snapshot dated 2026-11-21, the Wayback Machine / IANA archive copy of https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types captured on or before that date is the artefact to exhibit. That step affects only the provenance of the exhibit, not the answer: any 'example' subtype appearing there would itself be a violation of RFC 4735 §3 and would have to be treated as an erratum, not as a registration.

4. DISAMBIGUATION THE REVIEWER WILL NEED (frequent source of error)

There are two different things, and conflating them produces a wrong compliance finding:

  • Subtypes UNDER the 'example' top-level type — `example/<anything>`. None registered; none registrable. (The question asked.)

  • The eight subtypes NAMED 'example' under OTHER top-level types, registered by RFC 4735 §4: `application/example`, `audio/example`, `image/example`, `message/example`, `model/example`, `multipart/example`, `text/example`, `video/example`. These ARE registered (published specification: RFC 4735; intended usage: LIMITED USE; change controller: IETF). Each has its own IANA registration page, e.g. https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/multipart/example, whose template reads: "Type name: 'application', 'audio', 'image', 'message', 'model', 'multipart', 'text', and 'video'. Subtype name: 'example'." They are */*example* forms, not *example/** forms.

So "is there a registered example subtype?" has answer yes for `text/example` and its seven siblings, and answer no for anything of the form `example/*`. The compliance question as posed ("subtype under the IANA 'example' media type") is the second case.

5. WHAT THE REVIEWER SHOULD ACTUALLY PUT IN THE NEW DOCUMENTATION EXAMPLE

Given the rule, any of the following is correct and compliant; none requires or admits an IANA registration:

  Option A (free-form, matches the registry's own wording): use `example/` followed by any syntactically valid subtype token, e.g. `example/foo`, `example/notification-v2`. RFC 4735 §3: "any subtype may be used with the 'example' type." Parameters, encoding considerations, etc. are "as invented by the user."

  Option B (uses an actual registration): use one of the RFC 4735 §4 subtypes under a real top-level type, e.g. `application/example` or `text/example`, when the example concerns a subtype of that specific type.

  Option C (non-standards trees): RFC 4735 §1 suggests that compilers of illustrative examples involving media types in trees other than the standards tree "might also incorporate the string 'example' into their hypothetical media types." This is a suggestion, not a registration.

Mandatory caveats to attach to any such example:

  • The 'example' type and its subtypes are for documentation only and MUST NOT be implemented (RFC 4735 §3, §4).
  • Their appearance in real code can lead to unpredictable results and open security holes (RFC 4735 §4, security considerations).
  • Any attempt to negotiate or send one of these example subtypes is bound to lead to interoperability problems (RFC 4735 §4).
  • The occurrence of an 'example' media type outside of examples — e.g. in a live Content-Type header — "is an error and should be reported to the implementor" (IANA registry note).
  • A document or product that emits `example/...` in production traffic is non-conformant; the finding is against the implementation, not against the registry.

6. HOW TO REPRODUCE AND AUDIT THIS FINDING (for the compliance file)

Step 1. Open https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types and locate the 'example' section. Confirm the note text in §2.1 above, in particular the sentence "No subtype can be registered with IANA."

Step 2. Open https://www.iana.org/assignments/top-level-media-types and confirm the 'example' row: Reference RFC 4735, Registry of Subtypes "Example Media Types", Comments "no registrations, for examples only", Last Updated 2025-03-18.

Step 3. Confirm the prohibition at source: RFC 4735 §3, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4735 ("IANA MUST NOT register any subtypes for the 'example' media type").

Step 4. Check that no successor RFC supersedes RFC 4735 for the 'example' type. Test: if a successor existed, the top-level registry's Reference column for 'example' would name it; it names RFC 4735. This is the kill condition for the finding — if the Reference column ever shows a document other than RFC 4735, re-run the analysis against that document.

Step 5. If a dated exhibit is required, capture an archive copy of Step 1's page with a timestamp on or before 2026-11-21; the substantive content will match.

7. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER

Only one thing: a new Standards-Track RFC that supersedes RFC 4735 and relaxes or removes the MUST NOT in its §3, followed by IANA populating an 'example' subtype registry (the 'example' row would then link a populated "Example Media Types" registry instead of stating "no registrations, for examples only"). Absent that, the number of registered `example/*` subtypes is zero on 2026-11-21 and on every date the rule remains in force. No such document appears in any source consulted for this review.
