ANSWER

1) Name of the bound: ub-emailaddress-length
2) Old value (RFC 3280): 128 — New value (RFC 5280): 255

VERBATIM AUTHORITY (RFC 5280, 'Changes from RFC 3280' / introduction):

  "The ASN.1 modules in Appendix A are unchanged from RFC 3280, except
   that ub-emailaddress-length was changed from 128 to 255 in order to
   align with PKCS #9 [RFC2985]."

This sentence is the direct, unambiguous statement of the change and is reproduced identically on every mirror fetched (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html, docs.ldap.com RFC 5280 text, datatracker.ietf.org RFC 5280, rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5280).

MODULE-LEVEL CORROBORATION (the two Appendix A modules themselves, PKIX1Explicit88 'Upper Bounds' block):

  RFC 5280:  ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 255
  RFC 3280:  ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 128

Same identifier, same position in the upper-bounds block, differing only in the value — exactly the one-line delta RFC 5280 announces.

CORRECTION TO THE PROJECT-CONTEXT ASSUMPTION (important — do not carry the assumption forward)

The project context pre-supposed the bound was ub-pseudonym, 'raised from 128 in RFC 3280 to 255 in RFC 5280'. That is wrong, and the same fetched ASN.1 modules disprove it: both RFC 3280 and RFC 5280 contain

  ub-pseudonym INTEGER ::= 128

ub-pseudonym is 128 in both documents; it did not change. Any deliverable built on the ub-pseudonym assumption would name a bound that RFC 5280 explicitly says is unchanged, and would contradict the RFC's own change log. The correct bound is ub-emailaddress-length.

SINGLE-CHANGE VERIFICATION (diff of the two upper-bounds blocks as quoted)

Comparing the two 'Upper Bounds' blocks line by line, every bound is identical between RFC 3280 and RFC 5280 except one:

  ub-name 32768; ub-common-name 64; ub-locality-name 128; ub-state-name 128;
  ub-organization-name 64; ub-organizational-unit-name 64; ub-title 64;
  ub-serial-number 64; ub-match 128; ub-common-name-length 64;
  ub-country-name-alpha-length 2; ub-country-name-numeric-length 3;
  ub-domain-defined-attributes 4; ub-domain-defined-attribute-type-length 8;
  ub-domain-defined-attribute-value-length 128; ub-domain-name-length 16;
  ub-extension-attributes 256; ub-e163-4-number-length 15;
  ub-e163-4-sub-address-length 40; ub-generation-qualifier-length 3;
  ub-given-name-length 16; ub-initials-length 5; ub-integer-options 256;
  ub-numeric-user-id-length 32; ub-organization-name-length 64;
  ub-organizational-unit-name-length 32; ub-organizational-units 4;
  ub-pds-name-length 16; ub-pds-parameter-length 30;
  ub-pds-physical-address-lines 6; ub-postal-code-length 16;
  ub-pseudonym 128; ub-surname-length 40; ub-terminal-id-length 24;
  ub-unformatted-address-length 180; ub-x121-address-length 16   -- all identical
  ub-emailaddress-length: 128 (RFC 3280) -> 255 (RFC 5280)      -- the only difference

This confirms the RFC's 'unchanged ... except' wording and confirms there is exactly one answer to the question.

SEMANTICS OF THE BOUND (for implementers)

- ub-emailaddress-length is the ASN.1 upper bound (in characters) on the emailAddress attribute value and on the rfc822Name-style e-mail address string used by the PKIX name forms; the Appendix A note states upper bounds on string types are measured in characters, and that for IA5String/PrintableString the octet count equals the character count.
- Practical effect of the change: the maximum e-mail address length permitted in a conforming certificate/attribute goes from 128 to 255 characters.
- The alignment source named by RFC 5280 is PKCS #9, cited as [RFC2985]. (RFC 2985 itself was not among the pages fetched for this answer, so its internal ub-emailaddress-length value is reported here only as the reference RFC 5280 names, not as independently re-verified text.)

PROCEDURE TO REPRODUCE THE RESULT (no tooling assumed; any text editor or grep suffices)

1. Open RFC 5280 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html), search for the string 'align with PKCS #9'. Read the surrounding paragraph — it names ub-emailaddress-length and states 128 -> 255.
2. In the same document, go to Appendix A.1 (PKIX1Explicit88), locate the 'Upper Bounds' block, and confirm 'ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 255'.
3. Open RFC 3280 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3280.txt), go to Appendix A.1, same 'Upper Bounds' block, and confirm 'ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 128'.
4. Cross-check the distractor: confirm 'ub-pseudonym INTEGER ::= 128' appears in both documents (i.e., unchanged).
5. Record: name = ub-emailaddress-length; old = 128; new = 255.

STATUS OF THE TWO ASKS

Ask 1: answered — ub-emailaddress-length (identifier, no unit).

answer:
# What the LIMIT clause bounds in SPARQL 1.1

## Answer (one line)

**LIMIT puts an upper bound on the number of solutions returned** — i.e. on the length of the solution sequence that the query's solution modifiers produce, measured *after* OFFSET has been applied. It does not bound triples matched, triples in a CONSTRUCT/DESCRIBE graph, RDF terms, bytes, or the amount of work the engine performs.

## Normative source text (verbatim)

Authority: **W3C Recommendation, SPARQL 1.1 Query Language, 21 March 2013** — `https://www.w3.org/TR/2013/REC-sparql11-query-20130321/` (identical text at `https://www.w3.org/TR/sparql11-query/`, the "latest version" URL).

Section **15.5 LIMIT**:

> "The LIMIT clause puts an upper bound on the number of solutions returned. If the number of actual solutions, after OFFSET is applied, is greater than the limit, then at most the limit number of solutions will be returned."
>
> "A LIMIT of 0 would cause no results to be returned. A limit may not be negative."

Section **18.1.9 Solution Sequence Modifiers**:

> "Limit modifier: restrict the number of solutions"

Section **15.4 OFFSET** (context for the ordering/slicing interaction):

> "OFFSET causes the solutions generated to start after the specified number of solutions. An OFFSET of zero has no effect."
>
> "Using LIMIT and OFFSET to select different subsets of the query solutions will not be useful unless the order is made predictable by using ORDER BY."

Version note (for anyone reconciling drafts): the 2010-01-26 WD (§12.5), 2010-06-01 WD (§13.5), 2011-05-12-era WD (§13.5) and 2012-01-05 WD (§15.5) all carry the same first sentence — "The LIMIT clause puts an upper bound on the number of solutions returned." — but their second sentence reads "If the number of actual solutions is greater than the limit, ..." **without** the clause "after OFFSET is applied". The 2013 Recommendation adds that clause. Cite the Recommendation; the added clause is the authoritative clarification that OFFSET is applied first and LIMIT bounds what remains.

## What is actually bounded, stated precisely

Let Ω be the solution sequence produced by evaluating the graph pattern, then applying the solution modifiers in the spec's order. LIMIT of *k* bounds |result| — the cardinality of the returned sequence — not any property of the data.

| Bounded by LIMIT | Not bounded by LIMIT |
|---|---|
| Number of solutions (result rows) returned | Number of triples/graph patterns matched during evaluation |
| The length of the final solution sequence at that query level | Number of triples in a CONSTRUCT/DESCRIBE output graph |
| The count after OFFSET is applied | Number of distinct RDF terms mentioned |
| The count after DISTINCT/REDUCED and projection (see ordering below) | Bytes/characters of the serialized result |
| | Engine work (a conformant engine may scan arbitrarily many solutions to find the *k* it returns) |

## Algebra formalization

In the SPARQL algebra, LIMIT is one half of the **Slice** operator; OFFSET supplies the start index, LIMIT supplies the length:

```
Slice(Ω, start, length)
  start  = OFFSET value (default 0)
  length = LIMIT value  (unbounded if absent)
```

Semantics (paraphrase of the algebra definition in §18.5, not a verbatim quote): `Slice(Ω, start, length)` is the subsequence of Ω beginning at 0-based index `start` and containing at most `length` solutions. Consequences that follow directly:

- `length = 0` ⇒ empty sequence (matches "A LIMIT of 0 would cause no results to be returned").
- `start ≥ |Ω|` ⇒ empty sequence (OFFSET exhausts the sequence, so LIMIT has nothing left to bound).
- `|Ω| − start ≤ length` ⇒ the whole remainder is returned; LIMIT is an upper bound, not an exact count. The clause never *pads* a short result.

**Modifier application order** (from the spec's conversion of solution modifiers to algebra): grouping/aggregation → HAVING → VALUES → select expressions → `ToList` → `OrderBy` → `Project` → `Distinct` → `Reduced` → `Slice`. LIMIT is therefore applied **last**: it bounds the number of rows in the *final projected, de-duplicated* result, which is why `SELECT DISTINCT ... LIMIT 10` yields at most 10 *distinct* rows, and why LIMIT cannot be pushed below DISTINCT or projection without changing the answer.

## Interaction rules an implementer must get right

1. **ORDER BY + LIMIT.** Without ORDER BY the solution sequence is unordered, so *which* k solutions are returned is unspecified — any k is conformant. To make LIMIT select a deterministic subset you must ORDER BY first. This is exactly what §15.4 warns about.
2. **OFFSET + LIMIT.** OFFSET is applied first, then LIMIT bounds the remainder. `LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10` returns at most 5 solutions: positions 10–14 of the ordered sequence. LIMIT does *not* mean "stop after 15"; it means "take at most 5 after skipping 10".
3. **Subqueries.** Solution modifiers are per query level. A subquery's LIMIT bounds the solutions that level produces and that feed the outer pattern; an outer LIMIT independently bounds the outer level. `SELECT * { { SELECT ?x { ... } LIMIT 10 } ... } LIMIT 100` can return at most 10, not 100.
4. **CONSTRUCT / DESCRIBE.** LIMIT bounds the number of *solutions* used to instantiate the template/graph, not the number of triples in the output graph. One solution can instantiate several triples, and duplicate triples collapse in the RDF graph, so `|graph|` may be greater or smaller than the LIMIT value. Do not treat LIMIT as a triple-count cap.
5. **LIMIT 0 and negatives.** `LIMIT 0` is legal and returns no results. Negative limits are not permitted; the grammar restricts the operand to `INTEGER`, i.e. a non-negative integer literal.
6. **ASK (caution, not a normative claim).** The spec defines ASK in terms of whether the pattern has a solution; the LIMIT text is phrased in terms of solutions *returned*. No passage in hand settles whether `ASK ... LIMIT 0` must yield `false`, and implementations differ. Do not use `LIMIT 0` as a portable way to force an ASK to false.
7. **Server row caps are not LIMIT.** Engine/protocol-level maximum-row settings (Virtuoso `MaxRows`, endpoint result caps, `LIMIT`-injected by a proxy) are implementation extensions. They are not the LIMIT clause and do not carry its semantics (in particular they may truncate silently without any error, and they apply regardless of what the query asked for).

## Backend implementation guidance (query engine / API layer)

**Streaming cutoff (always safe).** Evaluate lazily and stop pulling solutions once *k* have been emitted, after OFFSET has been consumed. This is the reference implementation of the clause and is correct for every query shape; it saves work but does not change results.

**Pushdown safety rules.** Pushing LIMIT toward the source is only semantics-preserving when nothing between the source and the slice can change cardinality or order:

| Downstream operator present | May push LIMIT k down as… |
|---|---|
| none (plain BGP, no ORDER BY, no DISTINCT) | `LIMIT k` on the source scan |
| OFFSET m, no ORDER BY | `LIMIT k+m` on the source, then skip m |
| DISTINCT | must NOT push k; need k distinct rows, so push down `LIMIT k` only if the source is already distinct on the projected vars, otherwise push no limit (or push `k` only after de-dup) |
| ORDER BY | top-k: push an ordered scan with a bounded heap of size k (+m for OFFSET); never push an unordered LIMIT |
| aggregation / GROUP BY / HAVING | must NOT push; LIMIT applies to groups, not to input rows |
| joins | may push k to a join only if the join is cardinality-preserving on that side; in general push `LIMIT k` to the outermost join output |
| projection dropping variables | pushing below projection is fine for cardinality, but not if the projection feeds DISTINCT (see above) |

**SQL translation.** `LIMIT k OFFSET m` maps to `... ORDER BY <order> LIMIT k OFFSET m`. With no ORDER BY, emit the LIMIT without ORDER BY and treat row choice as unspecified — do not invent a deterministic order, since that would make results stable in a way the spec does not require and can hide missing ORDER BY in user queries. With ORDER BY, ensure the ORDER BY is fully deterministic (append a tiebreaker on all projected variables) if you want reproducible paging, and note that this is a stability guarantee your service adds, not one the spec grants.

**Paging contract for the API layer.** Because LIMIT bounds a slice of an *ordered* sequence, a paginated endpoint must reject or warn on `OFFSET`/page tokens without a total ordering; otherwise pages can silently duplicate or drop rows between requests. Enforce: (a) `limit ≥ 0`, reject negatives at parse/validation time with the same rule the grammar implies; (b) `limit = 0` short-circuits to an empty result without hitting the store; (c) a server-side hard cap should be reported explicitly to the caller (e.g. a truncation flag) rather than being confused with the user's LIMIT.

**Validation checklist for a review of a LIMIT implementation.**
1. LIMIT applies after OFFSET, after DISTINCT/REDUCED, after projection. 
2. LIMIT bounds solutions, not triples — verified separately for SELECT and CONSTRUCT paths.
3. `LIMIT 0` returns zero rows and does not error.
4. Negative limit is rejected, not clamped silently.
5. Subquery LIMIT is scoped to its own query level.
6. No pushdown of LIMIT across DISTINCT, aggregation, or an unordered ORDER BY.
7. LIMIT without ORDER BY is documented as non-deterministic in the service's API docs.

## Bottom line

LIMIT places an upper bound on **the number of solutions returned** — the cardinality of the solution sequence after OFFSET has been applied (and after ordering, projection and duplicate elimination), with `LIMIT 0` meaning "no results" and negative limits disallowed. Any framing of LIMIT as a cap on triples, terms, bytes, or engine work is incorrect.

Per RFC 8259 (The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format, Bray, Ed., STD 90, December 2017), Section 1 (Introduction):

  - Primitive types: 4  (string, number, boolean, null)
  - Structured types: 2  (object, array)

Verbatim source sentence (RFC 8259, §1, page 3):

  "JSON can represent four primitive types (strings, numbers, booleans,
   and null) and two structured types (objects and arrays)."

That single sentence is the authoritative statement for both asks; the numbers 4 and 2 are the RFC's own counts, not an inference.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. TYPE TABLE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

| # | Type     | Class      | RFC 8259 §3 ABNF production | Example          |
|---|----------|------------|-----------------------------|------------------|
| 1 | string   | primitive  | string                      | "a\u00e9"         |
| 2 | number   | primitive  | number                      | -12.5e+3         |
| 3 | boolean  | primitive  | false / true                | true             |
| 4 | null     | primitive  | null                        | null             |
| 5 | object   | structured | object                      | {"k":1}          |
| 6 | array    | structured | array                       | [1,2,3]          |

Totals: 4 primitive + 2 structured = 6 value types.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. SUPPORTING TEXT FROM THE RFC
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section 1 also defines the two structured types by construction, and in doing so enumerates the complete value domain:

  "An object is an unordered collection of zero or more name/value
   pairs, where a name is a string and a value is a string, number,
   boolean, null, object, or array.

   An array is an ordered sequence of zero or more values."

The 'value' enumeration in the object definition lists exactly six members: string, number, boolean, null, object, array — the same 4 + 2 partition. The two definitions are mutually consistent.

Section 3 (JSON Values) gives the grammar production, quoted exactly:

  value = false / null / true / object / array / number / string
  false = %x66.61.6c.73.65   ; false
  null  = %x6e.75.6c.6c      ; null
  true  = %x74.72.75.65      ; true
  object = begin-object [ member *( value-separator member ) ] end-object
  array = begin-array [ value *( value-separator value ) ] end-array

Section 2 (JSON Grammar) states: "A JSON text is a serialized value." So the six value types are exactly the set of legal top-level JSON texts as well as the set of legal nested values.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. RECONCILING COUNTS THAT LOOK DIFFERENT (guard against off-by-one reporting)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A reader comparing the §1 prose against the §3 grammar will see three different numbers. They are all correct, but they count different things. Use this table when reporting, so no downstream document states a count that contradicts another:

| Count | Number | What it counts                                              |
|-------|--------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| Primitive types            | 4 | Types: string, number, boolean, null                |
| Structured types           | 2 | Types: object, array                                |
| Total value types          | 6 | 4 + 2                                               |
| 'value' ABNF alternatives  | 7 | Productions: false, null, true, object, array, number, string |
| 'literal names' tokens (§2)| 3 | Tokens: false, null, true                           |
| Structural characters (§2) | 6 | Characters: { } [ ] : ,                            |

Why 7 ABNF alternatives still means 6 types: 'false' and 'true' are the two literals of the single boolean type. 7 alternatives - 1 (the duplicated boolean literal) = 6 types = 4 + 2. The §1 prose is the normative type taxonomy; the §3 grammar is the token-level encoding of it.

Why 'three literal names' is not 'three primitive types': §2 counts tokens ('strings, numbers, and three literal names'), where the three literal names are false, null, true. null is a type of its own; false and true are one type between them. So tokens (3 literal names + string + number) do not map 1:1 onto types.

Common wrong answers and why they are wrong:
  - '3 primitive types' — drops null, or collapses boolean into number.
  - '5 primitive types' — splits number into integer and floating point. RFC 8259 §6 defines a single 'number' grammar (int frac exp) and does not distinguish integer from floating point; that distinction belongs to implementations, not to JSON.
  - '2 boolean types' — true and false are literals of one type, not two types.
  - '6 primitive types' — treats objects/arrays as primitive; the RFC explicitly calls them structured.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. CORROBORATING SOURCE (independent wording)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

RFC 9535 (JSONPath), §1.1, restates the same taxonomy using RFC 8259's terminology:

  "The terms 'primitive' and 'structured' are used to group different
   kinds of values as in Section 1 of [RFC8259]. JSON objects and
   arrays are structured; all other values are primitive."

This confirms the partition is exhaustive and exclusive: {object, array} structured, {string, number, boolean, null} primitive, nothing outside the six.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. IMPLEMENTATION CHECKLIST (for a parser / schema validator / type mapper)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If this count is being used to size a type dispatch or a schema type enum, the six-case dispatch is:

  1. On the first significant byte, branch: '{' -> object, '[' -> array, '"' -> string, 't'/'f' -> boolean, 'n' -> null, '-' or digit -> number.
  2. Exactly six accepted cases; anything else is a syntax error (RFC 8259 §8.1: parsers MUST reject non-conforming text).
  3. Do not add a seventh case for integer vs. float at the JSON layer; if the application needs that distinction, it is a post-parse validation rule, not a JSON type.
  4. Do not treat duplicate member names as a distinct type; §4 leaves duplicate-name behavior to the implementation and notes it is unpredictable for interoperability.
  5. A JSON Schema 'type' enum derived from this taxonomy has exactly six values: "string", "number", "boolean", "null", "object", "array". ("integer" in JSON Schema is a semantic refinement of number, not a seventh JSON type.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. FINAL VALUES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Ask 1 — primitive types JSON can represent per RFC 8259: 4
  Ask 2 — structured types JSON can represent per RFC 8259: 2

Source: RFC 8259, §1, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.html#section-1>.

answer:
ANSWER

Maximum number of octets in a UTF-8 sequence for characters in U+0000..U+10FFFF under RFC 3629: 4 octets.

1. PRIMARY EVIDENCE — RFC 3629, Section 3 (UTF-8 definition)

RFC 3629 (Yergeau, 'UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646', Standards Track, November 2003) states directly:

  "In UTF-8, characters from the U+0000..U+10FFFF range (the UTF-16
   accessible range) are encoded using sequences of 1 to 4 octets."

and gives the format table:

  Char. number range  |        UTF-8 octet sequence
  (hexadecimal)       |              (binary)
  --------------------+---------------------------------------------
  0000 0000-0000 007F | 0xxxxxxx
  0000 0080-0000 07FF | 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx
  0000 0800-0000 FFFF | 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx
  0001 0000-0010 FFFF | 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx

The table terminates at the four-octet form. The last row's upper bound, 0010 FFFF, is exactly U+10FFFF, so the four-octet form is the longest sequence the RFC defines for the stated range. There is no five- or six-octet row.

2. WHY IT IS 4 AND NOT 5 OR 6 — RFC 3629, Section 12

Section 12, 'Changes from RFC 2279', lists as the first change:

  "o  Restricted the range of characters to 0000-10FFFF (the UTF-16
      accessible range)."

This is the operative edit. RFC 2279 (and RFC 2044 before it) encoded a 31-bit code space and therefore permitted sequences up to six octets. RFC 3629 capped the code space at U+10FFFF, which caps the encoding at four octets. Under RFC 3629 a five- or six-octet sequence is not merely discouraged — it is not well-formed UTF-8.

3. INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION FROM THE ABNF — RFC 3629, Section 4

Section 4 gives the normative grammar, which also stops at four octets:

  UTF8-octets = *( UTF8-char )
  UTF8-char   = UTF8-1 / UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
  UTF8-1      = %x00-7F
  UTF8-2      = %xC2-DF UTF8-tail
  UTF8-3      = %xE0 %xA0-BF UTF8-tail /
                %xE1-EC 2( UTF8-tail ) /
                %xED %x80-9F UTF8-tail /
                %xEE-EF 2( UTF8-tail )
  UTF8-4      = %xF0 %x90-BF 2( UTF8-tail ) /
                %xF1-F3 3( UTF8-tail ) /
                %xF4 %x80-8F 2( UTF8-tail )
  UTF8-tail   = %x80-BF

Notes on the bounds encoded in this grammar:
- UTF8-4 is the final alternative; no UTF8-5 or UTF8-6 production exists.
- The four-octet lead byte is restricted to %xF0-%xF4. %xF5-%xFF can never start a valid sequence.
- The %xF4 row admits only %x80-%x8F as its second octet, which is precisely the constraint that keeps the maximum code point at U+10FFFF (F4 8F BF BF).
- The %xF0 row admits only %x90-%xBF as its second octet, excluding overlong encodings below U+10000.
- The %xED row admits only %x80-%x9F as its second octet, excluding surrogates U+D800..U+DFFF.

4. ARITHMETIC CHECK (confirms 4 octets suffice and 5 are unnecessary)

Payload bits available per sequence length:
  1 octet : 7 bits                     -> 7 bits   (U+0000..U+007F)
  2 octets: 5 + 6 = 11 bits            -> 11 bits  (U+0080..U+07FF)
  3 octets: 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 bits        -> 16 bits  (U+0800..U+FFFF)
  4 octets: 3 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 21 bits    -> 21 bits  (U+10000..U+10FFFF)

U+10FFFF = 0x10FFFF = 1 0000 1111 1111 1111 1111 binary = 21 bits. The four-octet form's 21 payload bits exactly cover the code space ceiling, so four octets is both sufficient and the minimum sufficient length for the top of the range. Five octets (26 payload bits) would only be needed for code points above U+10FFFF, which RFC 3629 excludes.

Worked boundary encodings (each exactly 4 octets):
  U+10000  = F0 90 80 80
  U+10FFFF = F4 8F BF BF
For comparison, the largest three-octet encoding is U+FFFF = EF BF BF, and anything above it requires the four-octet form.

5. CORROBORATING SECONDARY SOURCES (consistent with the above)

- utf-8(7) (Debian manpages): "According to RFC 3629 no point above U+10FFFF should be used, which limits characters to four bytes." The same page notes the historical state of affairs: "UTF-8 encoded UCS characters may be up to six bytes long, however the Unicode standard specifies no characters above 0x10ffff, so Unicode characters can be only up to four bytes long in UTF-8."
- draft-hoffman-rfc3536bis (IETF terminology draft): "Characters in the BMP are encoded as one, two, or three octets. Characters outside the BMP are encoded as four octets."

6. SCOPE CAVEATS WORTH STATING EXPLICITLY

- The figure 4 is the maximum length of a well-formed UTF-8 sequence as defined by RFC 3629. It is not a buffer-size or application limit, and it is not affected by surrogates or noncharacters (which RFC 3629 excludes from valid sequences, further tightening rather than loosening the bound).
- The answer 4 applies to RFC 3629. Implementations that accept 5- or 6-octet sequences are following the obsolete RFC 2279/RFC 2044 encoding (IANA's retired 'UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8'), not 'UTF-8' as registered and standardized.
- No project-specific context alters the figure; it follows directly from the RFC's encoding rules.

BOTTOM LINE: 4 octets.

## Answer

**76 characters.** MIME (RFC 2045) limits a line of base64-encoded data to a maximum of 76 encoded characters, not counting the trailing CRLF line terminator.

## Primary citation

RFC 4648, §3.1 ("Line Feeds in Encoded Data"), states the proposition directly:

> "MIME [4] is often used as a reference for base 64 encoding. However, MIME does not define 'base 64' per se, but rather a 'base 64 Content-Transfer-Encoding' for use within MIME. As such, MIME enforces a limit on line length of base 64-encoded data to 76 characters."

RFC 4648 is here reporting a constraint owned by MIME, not defining one of its own — which is why the request's phrasing ("RFC 4648 says MIME enforces...") resolves to the same number either way. The normative source is RFC 2045 §6.8 (Base64 Content-Transfer-Encoding): the encoded output stream must be represented in lines of no more than 76 characters each, and all line breaks or characters not in the base64 alphabet are to be ignored by decoding software.

## Counting rule: CRLF is excluded

RFC 2045 §6.7 states the counting convention for the identical 76-character bound explicitly:

> "The 76 character limit does not count the trailing CRLF, but counts all other characters, including any equal signs."

The same convention applies to base64, and is reinforced by RFC 2045 §6.8's instruction that CRLF is not part of the base64 alphabet and must be ignored on decode, and by RFC 4648 §3.3, which classifies adjacent CRLF as "non-alphabet characters" that are ignored. Therefore:

- **Counted toward the 76:** all base64 alphabet characters (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, `+`, `/`) plus padding `=` characters.
- **Not counted:** the CRLF that terminates the line.

On the wire a maximal conformant line therefore occupies **78 octets** (76 + CR + LF).

## Why 76 — the arithmetic that keeps it consistent

- Base64 emits 4 characters per 3 input bytes.
- 76 is divisible by 4 (76 / 4 = **19**), so a 76-character line encodes exactly **19 quanta = 57 input bytes**, and line wrapping never splits a 4-character quantum or a padding group. 57 × 4/3 = 76 exactly.
- 76 + 2 (CRLF) = 78 octets, comfortably under the SMTP 1000-octet line ceiling (RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.6), which RFC 4648 §3.1 names as the origin of both the MIME and PEM limits ("The MIME and PEM limits are both due to limits within SMTP").
- A final line may be shorter than 76 and may carry one or two `=` padding characters; those `=` characters are inside the 76, not additional to it.

## Implementation constants and procedure

```
MIME_BASE64_MAX_LINE_CHARS = 76     # encoded characters, CRLF excluded
MIME_BASE64_LINE_TERMINATOR = "\r\n"
MIME_BASE64_INPUT_BYTES_PER_LINE = 57   # 76 / 4 * 3
```

Encoder (conformant MIME output):

```python
import base64

MAX = 76
CHUNK = 57  # 57 input bytes -> exactly 76 base64 chars

def mime_base64_encode(data: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(data), CHUNK):
        line = base64.b64encode(data[i:i + CHUNK])
        # CHUNK is a multiple of 3, so only the final chunk can carry padding
        assert len(line) <= MAX
        out.append(line)
    return b"\r\n".join(out) + (b"\r\n" if out else b"")
```

Invariants this code must maintain:

1. `len(line) <= 76` for every emitted line — asserted, not assumed.
2. Terminator is CRLF, never bare LF, in MIME transport contexts (RFC 2045 §2.7/§6.8).
3. No trailing whitespace, no tabs, no spaces inside a line.
4. The last line is the only one that may be shorter than 76 and the only one that may contain `=`.

Decoder (robust, per RFC 2045 §6.8 and RFC 4648 §3.3):

```python
def mime_base64_decode(text: bytes) -> bytes:
    # Strip CRLF and any other non-alphabet characters; MIME says ignore them.
    cleaned = bytes(c for c in text if c in _B64_ALPHABET or c == 0x3D)
    return base64.b64decode(cleaned, validate=False)
```

Decoder policy, stated explicitly so it is not left to interpretation:

- **Accept** lines longer than 76. Most deployed encoders and decoders do; RFC 2045 §6.8 says a robust implementation may decode and warn. Do not hard-fail on over-long lines in a receive path.
- **Reject** only on genuinely undecodable input (bad quantum length after cleaning, or more than two `=` at the end).
- **Warn** (log/metric) on over-long lines and on non-alphabet characters encountered, so non-conformant senders are visible without breaking interop.

## Test vectors

| Input bytes | Expected output | Check |
|---|---|---|
| 0 bytes | empty | no line emitted |
| 1 byte (`0x00`) | `AA==` + CRLF | short final line, padding counted inside 4 |
| 2 bytes | `AAA=` + CRLF | one `=` |
| 3 bytes | `AAAA` + CRLF | no padding |
| 57 bytes | exactly 76 chars + CRLF | maximal conformant line, 78 octets on wire |
| 58 bytes | 76 chars + CRLF, then 4 chars + CRLF | wrap boundary correct, quantum not split |
| 114 bytes | two 76-char lines | 2 × 57 bytes |

## Disambiguation table (why 76, not 64)

The neighbouring specs use different numbers; the request asks specifically for MIME:

| Spec | Line length | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **RFC 2045 (MIME) base64** | **76** | the answer; CRLF excluded from the count |
| RFC 2045 (MIME) quoted-printable | 76 | same figure, different encoding; CRLF excluded |
| RFC 1421 (PEM) | 64 | the ancestor encoding; RFC 4648 §3.1 notes MIME calls itself "virtually identical" to PEM but changes the line length |
| RFC 7468 (PKIX/PKCS/CMS textual) | 64 | modern PEM-like armor |
| RFC 9580 (OpenPGP armor) | 76 | |
| RFC 4648 §4 (plain base64) | no limit | RFC 4648 §3.1 forbids encoders from adding line feeds unless a referring spec says to |

A decoder or config that hard-codes 64 for MIME base64 is wrong by 12 characters; one that hard-codes 76 for PEM armor is wrong in the other direction. Keep the constant keyed to the content-transfer-encoding and the enclosing spec, not to "base64" generically.

# RFC 3339 hour values (profile of ISO 8601)

## 1. Answer

RFC 3339 permits exactly **24 hour values: `00` through `23` inclusive**, as a mandatory **two-digit** field. The value **`24` is not permitted**, even though ISO 8601 itself allows `24` (end-of-day).

Two independent statements in RFC 3339 (Klyne & Newman, July 2002) establish this:

**§5.6, the ABNF for the Internet Date/Time Format:**

```abnf
time-hour       = 2DIGIT  ; 00-23
time-minute     = 2DIGIT  ; 00-59
time-second     = 2DIGIT  ; 00-58, 00-59, 00-60 based on leap second
                          ; rules
time-secfrac    = "." 1*DIGIT
time-numoffset  = ("+" / "-") time-hour ":" time-minute
time-offset     = "Z" / time-numoffset
partial-time    = time-hour ":" time-minute ":" time-second [time-secfrac]
```

**§5.7, prose (the decisive sentence):**

> "Although ISO 8601 permits the hour to be \"24\", this profile of ISO 8601 only allows values between \"00\" and \"23\" for the hour in order to reduce confusion."

## 2. Enumerated set (24 values, `2DIGIT`)

| # | value | # | value | # | value | # | value |
|---|-------|---|-------|---|-------|---|-------|
| 1 | `00` | 7 | `06` | 13 | `12` | 19 | `18` |
| 2 | `01` | 8 | `07` | 14 | `13` | 20 | `19` |
| 3 | `02` | 9 | `08` | 15 | `14` | 21 | `20` |
| 4 | `03` | 10 | `09` | 16 | `15` | 22 | `21` |
| 5 | `04` | 11 | `10` | 17 | `16` | 23 | `22` |
| 6 | `05` | 12 | `11` | 18 | `17` | 24 | `23` |

Excluded: `24` (valid in ISO 8601, forbidden by this profile). Also excluded by the `2DIGIT` production: `0`–`9` (single digit), `000`–`023` (three digits), `+23`, `-00`, whitespace-padded forms.

## 3. Where `time-hour` occurs — both occurrences use 00–23

1. **Clock hour** of `partial-time` (the hour of the timestamp itself).
2. **Offset hour** of `time-numoffset` — the ABNF *reuses* `time-hour`, so the hour component of a numeric offset is also constrained to `00`–`23`; `+24:00`, `-25:30` are invalid, while `+00:20` (RFC 3339's own Netherlands example) is valid.

Note that the offset *sign-and-zero* case `-00:00` is legal ("unknown local offset") and is a property of `time-numoffset`, not a widening of the hour set.

## 4. Interaction with leap seconds (does NOT widen the hour set)

The leap-second special case lives in `time-second` (`00-60`), not in `time-hour`. Two consequences worth stating precisely, because they are the usual source of bugs:

- The hour field of a leap-second timestamp is still one of `00`–`23`. RFC 3339's example `1990-12-31T23:59:60Z` uses hour `23`; `1990-12-31T15:59:60-08:00` uses hour `15` — the *same* instant expressed 8 hours behind UTC. **Do not** hard-code "second 60 implies hour 23": with a non-zero offset the leap second lands on a different local hour (still within 00–23).
- The correct semantic rule is: second `60` is valid only when the instant, normalised to UTC, is `23:59:60` on 30 June or 31 December (per §5.7 leap-second rules). Enforce this in the *semantic* layer, not by touching the hour grammar.

## 5. Contrast with ISO 8601 (why the question is worth asking)

- ISO 8601 permits `24` (typically as `24:00:00` for end-of-day). RFC 3339 §5.7 removes it.
- RFC 3339 Appendix A ("ISO 8601 Collected ABNF") *does* admit hour `24` — e.g. `time-hour = 2DIGIT ; 00-24` — and even notes "ISO 8601 is not clear on whether an hour of 24 is permissible only if minutes and seconds are 0. This assumes that an hour of 24 is permissible in any context." **That appendix is informational and describes ISO 8601, not this profile.** Implementations must not derive the hour bound from Appendix A; the binding text is §5.6/§5.7.
- RFC 3339 is a conformant *subset* of the ISO 8601 *extended* format: separators are mandatory, fields are fixed-width, basic (separator-free) format is not part of the profile.

## 6. Reference validators

### 6.1 Hour-field predicate

```python
import re

# Exactly the 24 values 00-23; nothing else.
HOUR_RE = re.compile(r"\A(?:[01][0-9]|2[0-3])\Z")

def valid_hour(h: str) -> bool:
    """True iff h is a syntactically valid RFC 3339 time-hour (00-23)."""
    return isinstance(h, str) and HOUR_RE.match(h) is not None
```

### 6.2 Full partial-time + offset validator (syntactic layer)

```python
import re

TIME_RE = re.compile(r"""
    \A
    (?P<hour>[01][0-9]|2[0-3]) :
    (?P<minute>[0-5][0-9]) :
    (?P<second>[0-5][0-9]|60)
    (?:\.(?P<secfrac>[0-9]+))?
    (?P<offset>Z|[+-](?P<ohour>[01][0-9]|2[0-3]):(?P<ominute>[0-5][0-9]))
    \Z
""", re.VERBOSE)

def parse_time(s: str):
    m = TIME_RE.match(s)
    if not m:
        return None
    return {
        "hour": int(m["hour"]),
        "minute": int(m["minute"]),
        "second": int(m["second"]),
        "offset": m["offset"],
    }
```

Note that the offset hour group uses the identical alternation `[01][0-9]|2[0-3]`, so the two `time-hour` occurrences cannot drift apart.

### 6.3 Semantic layer: leap-second placement

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def leap_second_ok(hour: int, minute: int, second: int,
                   offset: str) -> bool:
    """second == 60 is only legal at 23:59:60 UTC on 30 Jun / 31 Dec."""
    if second != 60:
        return True
    if offset == "Z":
        off = timedelta(0)
    else:
        sign = 1 if offset[0] == "+" else -1
        hh, mm = int(offset[1:3]), int(offset[4:6])
        off = sign * timedelta(hours=hh, minutes=mm)
    # Shift local wall clock back to UTC using only the time-of-day part.
    local = timedelta(hours=hour, minutes=minute)
    utc = (local - off) % timedelta(days=1)
    return utc == timedelta(hours=23, minutes=59)
```

## 7. Conformance test vectors

| input | hour field | expected | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `00:00:00Z` | `00` | accept | lower bound |
| `23:59:59Z` | `23` | accept | upper bound |
| `12:34:56.789-08:00` | `12` | accept | mid-range |
| `09:00:00+05:30` | `09` | accept | leading zero required and present |
| `23:59:60Z` | `23` | accept (semantic) | leap second at 23:59:60 UTC |
| `15:59:60-08:00` | `15` | accept (semantic) | same leap second, offset local hour |
| `24:00:00Z` | `24` | **reject** | ISO 8601 allows, this profile does not |
| `24:00:00-08:00` | `24` | **reject** | same rule, offset irrelevant |
| `9:00:00Z` | `9` | **reject** | not `2DIGIT` |
| `023:00:00Z` | `023` | **reject** | not `2DIGIT` |
| `12:00:00+24:00` | `24` (offset) | **reject** | offset hour also 00–23 |
| `12:00:00+00:20` | `00` (offset) | accept | RFC 3339 §5.8 example offset |
| `12:00:00-00:00` | `00` (offset) | accept | unknown-local-offset convention |

## 8. Implementation checklist for downstream code

1. Parse the hour as a fixed two-character slice, never as a free-form integer — `2DIGIT` is a *format* requirement, so `9:00:00Z` must be rejected even though the numeric value is in range.
2. Bound-check `0 <= h <= 23` after parsing; reject `24` explicitly and emit a distinct error code (e.g. `E_HOUR_24_ISO_ONLY`) so that diagnostics distinguish "ISO 8601 permits, RFC 3339 forbids" from a generic out-of-range failure.
3. Apply the *same* bound to the hour sub-field of numeric offsets.
4. Keep leap-second handling in a separate semantic pass keyed on `time-second == 60`, and validate it against the UTC-normalised instant (30 June / 31 December, 23:59:60 UTC). Do not encode leap seconds into the hour bound.
5. Do not accept basic-format timestamps (`19960412T232050Z`) or omitted separators; the profile is the *extended* format with mandatory punctuation.

RFC 6902 (JSON Patch), Section 4 "Operations" — allowed values for an operation object's "op" member

Normative text (RFC 6902, §4, verbatim):

  "Operation objects MUST have exactly one \"op\" member, whose value indicates the operation to perform. Its value MUST be one of \"add\", \"remove\", \"replace\", \"move\", \"copy\", or \"test\"; other values are errors."

1. The complete allowed value set (exactly six members, closed set)

  | # | "op" value | Defining section |
  |---|------------|------------------|
  | 1 | "add"      | RFC 6902 §4.1    |
  | 2 | "remove"   | RFC 6902 §4.2    |
  | 3 | "replace"  | RFC 6902 §4.3    |
  | 4 | "move"     | RFC 6902 §4.4    |
  | 5 | "copy"     | RFC 6902 §4.5    |
  | 6 | "test"     | RFC 6902 §4.6    |

  Enum (RFC order): ["add", "remove", "replace", "move", "copy", "test"]

2. Properties of the value set that a backend implementation must enforce

  a. Closed set / no extensions. RFC 6902 §4 says "other values are errors." There is no extension mechanism for "op" inside a document of media type application/json-patch+json. Any unrecognized value (e.g. "merge", "inc", "patch", "insert") is a hard error, not an ignorable member.

  b. Case-sensitive, lowercase only. The literals are defined in lowercase; since "other values are errors," "Add", "ADD", "Test" etc. are invalid. Compare with an exact string match, never a case-insensitive or trimmed comparison (do not trim whitespace, do not Unicode-normalize beyond what the JSON parser already did — the literal must be byte-for-byte one of the six ASCII strings).

  c. Type. The value MUST be a JSON string. `{"op": 1, ...}`, `{"op": null, ...}`, `{"op": ["add"], ...}` are all errors.

  d. Cardinality. "MUST have exactly one \"op\" member": missing "op" is an error; a duplicate "op" key in the same object is an error (RFC 6902 §4 requires exactly one, so an implementation that silently keeps the last-wins parse result is non-conforming for patch documents). Duplicate detection must happen at parse time, before the enum check.

  e. Distinguish unknown members from unknown op values. §4 states that members "not explicitly defined for the operation in question MUST be ignored (i.e., the operation will complete as if the undefined member did not appear in the object)" — so `{"op":"remove","path":"/a","value":1}` is valid and the stray "value" is ignored. This leniency applies to *members*, never to the *value of "op"*.

  f. Member order is not significant; `{"op":"add","path":"/a","value":1}` and `{"value":1,"path":"/a","op":"add"}` are equivalent.

3. Companion members required per op (needed to validate an operation object once "op" is accepted; §4 and §4.1-4.6)

  | "op"    | "path" | "value"        | "from"         | Other constraints |
  |---------|--------|----------------|----------------|-------------------|
  | add     | required | required      | ignored        | target must be root, an existing object member to add, or an array index / "-" |
  | remove  | required | ignored       | ignored        | target location MUST exist |
  | replace | required | required      | ignored        | target location MUST exist |
  | move    | required | ignored       | required       | "from" MUST exist; "from" MUST NOT be a proper prefix of "path" |
  | copy    | required | ignored       | required       | "from" MUST exist |
  | test    | required | required      | ignored        | target MUST exist and be equal to "value" (type-strict equality per §4.6) |

  ("path" is required for every op, per §4: "operation objects MUST have exactly one \"path\" member.")

4. Machine-checkable schema (JSON Schema 2020-12) for an operation object

  {
    "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
    "$id": "https://example.internal/schema/json-patch-operation.json",
    "title": "RFC 6902 operation object",
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["op", "path"],
    "properties": {
      "op":   { "enum": ["add", "remove", "replace", "move", "copy", "test"] },
      "path": { "type": "string" },
      "from": { "type": "string" },
      "value": {}
    },
    "allOf": [
      { "if": { "properties": { "op": { "const": "add" } }, "required": ["op"] },
        "then": { "required": ["path", "value"] } },
      { "if": { "properties": { "op": { "const": "remove" } }, "required": ["op"] },
        "then": { "required": ["path"] } },
      { "if": { "properties": { "op": { "const": "replace" } }, "required": ["op"] },
        "then": { "required": ["path", "value"] } },
      { "if": { "properties": { "op": { "const": "move" } }, "required": ["op"] },
        "then": { "required": ["path", "from"] } },
      { "if": { "properties": { "op": { "const": "copy" } }, "required": ["op"] },
        "then": { "required": ["path", "from"] } },
      { "if": { "properties": { "op": { "const": "test" } }, "required": ["op"] },
        "then": { "required": ["path", "value"] } }
    ]
  }

  Note: the schema above cannot express "exactly one 'op' member" (JSON Schema sees only the post-parse object); duplicate-key rejection must be done by the JSON parser (e.g. Jackson STRICT_DUPLICATE_DETECTION, Python object_pairs_hook, serde duplicate-field deny).

5. Validation procedure (ordering matters for correct error reporting)

  Step 1. Parse the patch document as JSON with duplicate-key detection enabled. On duplicate keys -> error 400, code "duplicate_member".
  Step 2. The document MUST be a JSON array (§3); each element MUST be an object. Else -> error, code "invalid_patch_document".
  Step 3. For each operation object:
    3a. If "op" absent -> error, code "missing_op".
    3b. If "op" is not a string -> error, code "invalid_op_type".
    3c. If "op" not in {add, remove, replace, move, copy, test} -> error, code "invalid_op_value" (include the offending value and the allowed set in the error payload).
    3d. If "path" absent or not a string -> error, code "missing_or_invalid_path".
    3e. Apply the per-op required-member table in §3 above; missing "value"/"from" -> error, code "missing_required_member".
    3f. Structural checks (index bounds, from-prefix-of-path for move, target existence for remove/replace/test) -> errors per §4.x and §5.
  Step 4. Apply operations sequentially and atomically (§3, §5): if any operation fails, the whole patch fails and the target document is left unmodified.

6. Reference implementation of the enum check

  const OP_VALUES = Object.freeze(['add', 'remove', 'replace', 'move', 'copy', 'test']);

  function validateOp(op) {
    if (op === undefined) throw new PatchError('missing_op');
    if (typeof op !== 'string') throw new PatchError('invalid_op_type');
    if (!OP_VALUES.includes(op)) {            // exact, case-sensitive
      throw new PatchError('invalid_op_value', { got: op, allowed: OP_VALUES });
    }
    return op;
  }

  Equivalent SQL/enum if the op is persisted:
    CREATE TYPE json_patch_op AS ENUM ('add','remove','replace','move','copy','test');
  (Postgres enums compare case-sensitively and reject anything outside the label set, matching RFC semantics; note that adding a label later would require a migration, which is correct — RFC 6902 does not permit new op values without a new specification.)

7. Acceptance / rejection test vectors

  Accepted (op value):
    {"op":"add","path":"/a/b/c","value":"foo"}      -> valid
    {"op":"remove","path":"/a/b/c"}                  -> valid
    {"op":"replace","path":"/a/b/c","value":42}      -> valid
    {"op":"move","from":"/a/b/c","path":"/a/b/d"}   -> valid
    {"op":"copy","from":"/a/b/c","path":"/a/b/e"}   -> valid
    {"op":"test","path":"/a/b/c","value":"foo"}     -> valid
    {"value":"foo","path":"/a/b/c","op":"add"}      -> valid (member order irrelevant)
    {"op":"remove","path":"/a","value":1}            -> valid (undefined member ignored)

  Rejected (op value):
    {"op":"Add","path":"/a","value":1}       -> invalid_op_value (case)
    {"op":"ADD","path":"/a","value":1}       -> invalid_op_value (case)
    {"op":"merge","path":"/a","value":1}     -> invalid_op_value (not in set)
    {"op":"patch","path":"/a"}               -> invalid_op_value (not in set)
    {"op":"","path":"/a"}                    -> invalid_op_value
    {"op":" add","path":"/a","value":1}      -> invalid_op_value (leading space)
    {"op":1,"path":"/a"}                      -> invalid_op_type
    {"op":null,"path":"/a"}                   -> invalid_op_type
    {"path":"/a","value":1}                   -> missing_op
    {"op":"add","op":"remove","path":"/a"}    -> duplicate_member

Answer to the ask: the allowed values are "add", "remove", "replace", "move", "copy", and "test" — six values, no others.

RFC 4648 base64 (Section 4) calculation for 9 octets:

1. 9 octets = 9 × 8 = 72 bits.
2. Base64 processes each 24-bit input quantum into 4 output characters of 6 bits each.
3. 72 bits / 24 bits = 3 complete quanta, remainder 0.
4. 3 × 4 = 12 encoded characters. Equivalently, 72 / 6 = 12 six-bit groups.
5. Because the final quantum is an integral multiple of 24 bits, RFC 4648 Section 4 case (1) applies: the final unit of encoded output is an integral multiple of 4 characters with no '=' padding. Therefore the output is 12 data characters and 0 pad characters.

Default padding rule, RFC 4648 Section 3.2: 'Implementations MUST include appropriate pad characters at the end of encoded data unless the specification referring to this document explicitly states otherwise.' Section 3.2 also notes that in some circumstances padding is not required or used, but in the general case, when assumptions about the size of transported data cannot be made, padding is required to yield correct decoded data. For base64, padding uses '='. The Section 4 cases are: 0 '=' when the final quantum is a 24-bit multiple; 2 '=' when the final quantum is exactly 8 bits; and 1 '=' when the final quantum is exactly 16 bits. For 9 octets, the applicable case is 0 '='.

Answer: 9 octets produce 12 encoded base64 characters in total. The default rule is that implementations MUST include appropriate '=' pad characters at the end of encoded data unless the specification referring to RFC 4648 explicitly states otherwise.

question: Y63
answer:
RFC 8785 (JCS) §3.2.4 ('UTF-8 Generation') requires the result of the preceding serialization step to be encoded in UTF-8. The final canonical output is therefore a UTF-8 byte sequence; UTF-16, UTF-32, Latin-1, and ASCII-only renderings are non-conforming. No BOM is emitted: EF BB BF would prepend an extra U+FEFF that is not part of the serialized JSON text and would change the bytes hashed or signed. The output starts at the first byte of the first JSON token.

U+000B is inside the ASCII control range U+0000..U+001F. The only short escapes are U+0008 -> \b, U+0009 -> \t, U+000A -> \n, U+000C -> \f, and U+000D -> \r. U+000B is not in that set, and JSON has no \v escape, so RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2's fallback applies: lowercase hexadecimal Unicode notation with exactly four hex digits. U+000B therefore serializes as the six-character sequence backslash, 'u', '0', '0', '0', 'b' -- \u000b -- whose UTF-8 bytes are 5C 75 30 30 30 62. Uppercase \u000B, \v, and a raw 0x0B byte inside the string are non-conforming.

String-escape procedure (for values and property names):
1. cp U+0008, U+0009, U+000A, U+000C, U+000D -> backslash followed by b, t, n, f, r respectively.
2. Any other cp in U+0000..U+001F -> backslash + 'u' + cp as four lowercase hex digits, zero-padded. Thus U+000B -> \u000b.
3. cp U+005C -> two backslashes; cp U+0022 -> backslash + double quote.
4. All other cp -> emit unchanged; enclose the whole sequence in double quotes; encode the result as UTF-8.

Minimal check: a property 'k' whose value is U+000B canonicalizes to {"k":"\u000b"} (no spaces), with UTF-8 bytes 7B 22 6B 22 3A 22 5C 75 30 30 30 62 22 7D.
